"q-94046" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}-10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-7.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-7.$ Computing $A-(-7)I,$ we get

$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}16 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -4{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},
$$

$$

P=[\begin{aligned}\,∗\, & 0 \\ \,∗\, & -1\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. $$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Find $f^{-1}(x)$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{4}{(x-1)^2}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{4}{(y-1)^2}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (4)/((y - 1)^{2}) \\
x \cdot (y - 1)^{2} &= 4 \\
(y - 1)^{2} &= \frac{4}{x} \\
\sqrt{(y - 1)^{2}} &= \sqrt{\frac{4}{x}} \\
\mid y - 1 \mid &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} \\
y - 1 &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} \\
y &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that for $y > 1$, we have

$$
\mid y-1 \mid = y-1
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} + 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048963} {:db/id 17592186049636} {:db/id 17592186050908} {:db/id 17592186193007 :question/id #uuid "3c59175d-f52e-5041-89a5-4b75797aab41" :question/math-academy-id "q-148295"} inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-x}{x+3}$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{2-x}{x+3}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{2-y}{y+3}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{2 - y}{y + 3} \\
x(y + 3) &= 2 - y \\
xy + 3x &= 2 - y \\
xy + y &= 2 - 3x \\
y(x + 1) &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{x + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{x+1}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051079} {:db/id 17592186193009 :question/id #uuid "3fbadf4f-ad61-5c64-abef-b812903e691b" :question/math-academy-id "q-148297"} {:db/id 17592186193020 :question/id #uuid "e69f0bd0-3d4a-57f7-adf5-e7456cb05052" :question/math-academy-id "q-148500"} {:db/id 17592186233503 :question/id #uuid "df275beb-4a97-5b5f-8143-53a9df6091e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-148506"} {:db/id 17592186233504 :question/id #uuid "09439e98-9680-5cbd-876f-1f24d85d22d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-148512"} {:db/id 17592186390552 :question/id #uuid "212d9c4b-4962-5204-87c1-b501c43df724" :question/math-academy-id "q-276773"} {:db/id 17592186192816 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192407 :question/id #uuid "f6ab6606-77ce-583a-9712-175825864612" :question/math-academy-id "e-10461"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dcedd9d0-f87c-58b2-9ef1-c9fa0ef2e5c1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193010 :question/id #uuid "08d61d78-0894-5a3b-a7fb-a0e5175e00e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-148298"} {:db/id 17592186193011 :question/id #uuid "5d4ef38d-4b7a-5aa7-8c47-cb116b290971" :question/math-academy-id "q-148300"} {:db/id 17592186233505 :question/id #uuid "651e4bfb-5157-5d68-a7ba-a294abf0647a" :question/math-academy-id "q-148536"} {:db/id 17592186233506 :question/id #uuid "7a603d75-6ffd-59b0-9266-98db796998e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-148544"} {:db/id 17592186294877 :question/id #uuid "424480f5-f543-5930-b060-4a890b9488ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-276793"}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining an Unknown Value Given the Inverse of a Rational Function"} {:db/id 17592186192407 :question/id #uuid "f6ab6606-77ce-583a-9712-175825864612" :question/math-academy-id "e-10461" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192816 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dcedd9d0-f87c-58b2-9ef1-c9fa0ef2e5c1" :knowledge-point/title "Determining an Unknown Value Given the Inverse of a Rational Function"}] :question/problem "The function $f(x)$, defined as
$f(x) = \dfrac{kx + 6}{x-4}, \qquad x\neq 4$
has an inverse function given by
$f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{4x+6}{x-2}, \qquad x\neq 2$.
What is the value of $k$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{kx + 6}{x-4}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{ky+6}{y-4}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{ky + 6}{y - 4} \\
x(y - 4) &= ky + 6 \\
xy - 4x &= ky + 6 \\
xy - ky &= 4x + 6 \\
y(x - k) &= 4x + 6 \\
y &= \frac{4x + 6}{x - k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{4x+6}{x-k}
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=2$."} {:db/id 17592186193010 :question/id #uuid "08d61d78-0894-5a3b-a7fb-a0e5175e00e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-148298"} {:db/id 17592186193011 :question/id #uuid "5d4ef38d-4b7a-5aa7-8c47-cb116b290971" :question/math-academy-id "q-148300"} {:db/id 17592186233505 :question/id #uuid "651e4bfb-5157-5d68-a7ba-a294abf0647a" :question/math-academy-id "q-148536"} {:db/id 17592186233506 :question/id #uuid "7a603d75-6ffd-59b0-9266-98db796998e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-148544"} {:db/id 17592186294877 :question/id #uuid "424480f5-f543-5930-b060-4a890b9488ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-276793"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186193719} :activity/id #uuid "b6520ec4-4c2b-5d03-b5d7-fdb5074438f4" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048898 :topic/id #uuid "ca45e315-1972-57c0-8e15-999d27a51d68" :topic/math-academy-id 3944} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186193719 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193826 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute inverses of reciprocal functions.

As an example, let's consider the function $f(x)$, given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{7}{2x+4}
$$

To find the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{7}{2x+4}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{7}{2y+4}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{7}{2y + 4} \\
x(2y + 4) &= 7 \\
2xy + 4x &= 7 \\
2xy &= 7 - 4x \\
y &= \frac{7 - 4x}{2x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{7 - 4x}{2x}

:tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute inverses of reciprocal functions.

As an example, let's consider the function $f(x)$, given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{7}{2x+4}
$$

To find the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{7}{2x+4}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{7}{2y+4}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{7}{2y + 4} \\
x(2y + 4) &= 7 \\
2xy + 4x &= 7 \\
2xy &= 7 - 4x \\
y &= \frac{7 - 4x}{2x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{7 - 4x}{2x}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1be3fc12-b770-5a76-ab56-1385a320d85f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6512 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c89b0360-91da-5424-aedb-da76a815447b" :step/math-academy-id 466026 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193720}} {:db/id 17592186193826 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute inverses of reciprocal functions.

That Lies on a Transformed Curve"}] :question/problem "The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y=x^4.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y = (x-2)^4-6?$ 

- $(a-2, b-6)$

- $(a+2,b+ 6)$

- $(a+2, b-6)$

- $(a-2,b+ 6)$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

To plot $y = (x-2)^4-6,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y=x^4.$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $2$ units to the right and get the graph of $y=(x-2)^4.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+2,b).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $6$ units down and obtain the graph of $y = (x-2)^4-6.$ After this transformation, the point $(a+2,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+2,b-6).
$$

**Method 2**

We are told that the point $(a, b)$ lies on the graph of $y = x^4$, which means:

$$
b=a^4
$$

Now, we want to find which point must lie on the graph of:

$$
y = (x-2)^4-6
$$

Let’s test what happens when we substitute $x = a + 2$ into this new equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(a+2-2{)}^{4}-6 \\  & ={a}^{4}-6 \\  & =b-6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, when $x = a + 2$, we get $y = b - 6.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186048753} {:db/id 17592186517170} {:db/id 17592186060003 :question/id #uuid "933f2dda-2343-544a-8ef3-2160dd14e9e2" :question/math-academy-id "q-121220"} {:db/id 17592186060258 :question/id #uuid "e4d7f8b8-ba0a-5db0-954f-1969ddfefa81" :question/math-academy-id "q-26398"} {:db/id 17592186233288 :question/id #uuid "00e41b54-1b06-55e4-ba21-6bbf8797df49" :question/math-academy-id "q-121381"} {:db/id 17592186233289 :question/id #uuid "7d1f17ba-35cc-58b5-9aa2-08d577267c2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-121393"} {:db/id 17592186233534 :question/id #uuid "4a80933c-10f7-51d8-9b1a-039e3550e2d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-158540" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059668 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0bd940e7-fccc-5811-b07a-11e4843b1785" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The point $(-1,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=3f(x+2)?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

To plot $y=3f(x+2),$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, shift the graph horizontally by $2$ unit to the left and get the graph of 
$y=f(x+2).$  After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1-2,1)=(-3,1).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the result by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the y-axis and get the graph of 
$y=3f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(-3,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-3,3\cdot 1)=(-3,3).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(-1,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$, we have that $f(-1)=1.$

Now consider the graph of $y=3f(x+2).$ Substituting $x=-3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3f(-3+2) \\  & =3f(-1) \\  & =3\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "The point $(3, 0)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x) - 1.$ What point **must** lie on $y = -f(x) + 3?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

To plot $y = -f(x) + 3,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y = f(x) - 1.$

- Then, we shift the graph by $1$ unit up and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(3,0)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(3,0+1)=(3,1).
$$

- Next, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(3,1)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(3,-(1)) = (3,-1).
$$

- Finally, shift the result by $3$ units up and obtain the graph of $y = -f(x) + 3.$ After this transformation, the point $(3,-1)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(3,-1+3)=(3,2).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(3, 0)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)-1$, we have that 

$$
f(3)-1 = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
f(3)=1.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y = -f(x) + 3.$ Substituting $x = 3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(3)+3 \\  & =-1+3 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(3, 2)$ must lie on $y = -f(x) + 3.$"} {:db/id 17592186517141} {:db/id 17592186060006 :question/id #uuid "35f6ccdb-baf2-5629-ace1-fbbc52cdd1b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-121405"} {:db/id 17592186060259 :question/id #uuid "49ac0e7b-6d64-5ad3-b75e-0edbe3724d3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-26595"} {:db/id 17592186233290 :question/id #uuid "66ee65e4-7115-5fe1-b74b-2344562d97c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-121431"} {:db/id 17592186233535 :question/id #uuid "1b6d8898-251c-5832-a715-c1e0b2d67196" :question/math-academy-id "q-158542" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059669 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "38b450bd-b43a-507c-9bbe-0aaf7a64a3ed" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve Given Another Transformed Curve"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The point  $(0,3)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x-1).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=f(x)+2?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

We first find a point corresponding to $(0,3)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=f(x)+2:$

- To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x-1).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally $1$ unit to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,3)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(0-1,3)=(-1,3).
$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=f(x)+2,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=f(x)+2.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,3)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(-1,3+2)=(-1,5).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(0,3)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x-1)$, we have that 

$$
f(0-1)=3\,⟹\,f(-1)=3.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=f(x)+2.$ Substituting $x=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(-1)+2 \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(-1,5)$ must lie on $y=f(x)+2.$"} {:db/id 17592186233536 :question/id #uuid "bcbd4637-6a8f-52c9-a823-7c7a1c3283b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-158546"} {:db/id 17592186233700 - stretching it by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $x$-axis, and then

- translating it by $1$ unit down.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the local maximum of $y=f(x)$ to the local maximum of $y=f(2x)-1.$ So, we need to find the image of $(2,6),$ the local maximum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation. 

To plot $y = f(2x)-1,$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(2,6).$

- Then, we stretch the result along the $x$-axis by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get the graph of $y=f(2x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,6)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2, 6 \right) = (1,6).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $1$ unit downward and get the graph of $y = f(2x)-1.$ After this transformation, the point $(1,6)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(1,6-1) = (1,5).
$$

Therefore, the local maximum of $y=f(2x)-1$ is $(1,5).$"} {:db/id 17592186048164} {:db/id 17592186050033} {:db/id 17592186517119} {:db/id 17592186060004 :question/id #uuid "bce89a1c-1788-5140-a53a-cfabf6eebe67" :question/math-academy-id "q-121221"} {:db/id 17592186060177 :question/id #uuid "1c0bb866-f5d6-5c26-9148-409419fa5279" :question/math-academy-id "q-186866"} {:db/id 17592186233626 :question/id #uuid "626e7d97-1fd4-5fea-b684-7fc6a67422d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-211287" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059670 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6eef35a-3502-5429-bd71-fb5bd0e8efc8" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Extrema on Transformed Curves"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/28/282e65324ea1e7893da25ead1cc822c7c166df880c3aecc60face9adbbb7279a.png)

:topic/math-academy-id 141} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060516 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060996 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that the point $( - 1 , 2 )$ lies on the graph of $y = f ( x ).$ What point *must* lie on the graph of $y = - f ( x ) + 3?$ This problem can be solved using one of two methods.

**Method 1 - Transform the Point Using Graph Transformations**

To plot $y = -f(x) + 3,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, we reflect the graph across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,2)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1,-(2)) = (-1,-2).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result by $3$ units up and obtain the graph of $y = -f(x) + 3.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,-2)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1,-2+3)={\color{blue}(-1,1)}.
$$

**Method 2 - Evaluate the Transformed Function**

Since the point $(-1, 2)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x),$ we have that $f(-1) = 2.$

Now, consider the graph of $y=-f(x)+3.$ Substituting $x = {\color{blue}-1}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(-1)+3 \\  & =-(2)+3 \\  & =-2+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $\color{blue}(-1, 1)$ must lie on $y = -f(x) + 3.$

So, both methods give the same result." :tutorial/id #uuid "1195d1cb-20e5-539e-beee-dfafe91b6953" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8400 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.3\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{15} \\ \frac{8}{15}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $q$ is a stochastic vector
- **II.** $Pq=q$
- **III.** $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
Pq=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{15} \\ \frac{8}{15}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1.4}{15}+\frac{5.6}{15} \\ \frac{5.6}{15}+\frac{2.4}{15}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{15} \\ \frac{8}{15}\end{bmatrix}=q.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector such that $Pq=q.$ So, it's a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186124771 :question/id #uuid "5d2ea1fa-42c3-5215-bede-8b745015a967" :question/math-academy-id "q-110239" :knowledge-point/_questions :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f53fa522-6d50-51d9-abdd-62735575a2d1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix"}] :question/problem "The table below describes how the customers of a particular electronics store feel about their next computer purchase.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Laptop** | **Desktop** |
| To: | **Laptop** | $0.9$ | $0.8$ |
| **Desktop** | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |  |

It is found that $10 \%$ of customers who currently use a laptop would choose a desktop on their next purchase, while $80 \%$ of customers who currently use a desktop would choose a laptop on their next purchase. 

Given that the store has $5\,400$ customers, all of whom purchase a new computer every two years, how many customers would eventually own a desktop computer if the given probabilities remain constant over many two-year periods?" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 
![](images/19/1935c4960a48e2b446c2610b9edc2a160a5f45462494c72a90f139ea2d13cc34.png)

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many two-year periods, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](images/29/29b5a209bb27b24f165ee418326763d8fb24f83f2b3a767052c381aa8cd0e01c.png)

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=8{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](images/0e/0e8f620c3392dbb77b1353184e38eaf48b526aa82c502772a5582bd20c7f5aea.png)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 9{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our steady-state vector is
![](images/2e/2ed7b0fc7296b2b651909c7c15c73e253fc8a9f95fb037072228d5de6f838894.png)

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{9}}}$ of the $5\,400$ customers would eventually own a desktop computer. Therefore, the total number of people who would eventually own a desktop computer is

$$
\dfrac{1}{9} \cdot 5\,400 = 600.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048853} {:db/id 17592186124772 :question/id #uuid "496d0736-5684-529d-8dd0-8b061c9a6089" :question/math-academy-id "q-110242" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124616 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f53fa522-6d50-51d9-abdd-62735575a2d1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "245874df-8c61-5865-89e0-2eea58d0ddb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186244636} {:answer/id #uuid "89ef273f-1ef4-5830-8401-02da27fbfef8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{7}" :db/id 17592186245524} {:answer/id #uuid "8f0491b5-2aa5-5777-aa10-2469c7c918ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{7}" :db/id 17592186245561} {:answer/id #uuid "b33e12af-527b-59a1-a8b0-87c0b7d8c14d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186245909} {:answer/id #uuid "d997fab9-f7e0-5e91-9d3c-7082d52b45a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186246248}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "89ef273f-1ef4-5830-8401-02da27fbfef8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{7}" :db/id 17592186245524} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c0a3814-685f-5c2a-a989-456250f0e6e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186246791}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & -0.1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{6}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{6}{7}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{1}{7}-\frac{6}{7}=-\frac{5}{7}.$"} {:db/id 17592186124774 :question/id #uuid "57c92fa7-df07-5594-a6b7-bd705bfe80a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-111172" :knowledge-point/_questions That is, $20%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities.

Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & -0.7\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{2}{9}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{7}{9}$ of the $9$ million population will live in cities. Therefore, the total number of people living in cities after many years will be

$$
\frac{7}{9}\cdot 9\,\text{million}=7\,\text{million}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269030 :question/id #uuid "d5136e32-dc7f-55de-b02b-4d944cd2c122" :question/math-academy-id "q-135323"} {:db/id 17592186269031 :question/id #uuid "2907c394-03b6-5c50-b20f-3b387f7ffb42" :question/math-academy-id "q-135324"} {:db/id 17592186269032 :question/id #uuid "1e24f728-ce2c-55b9-a28e-e90dcc5c4465" :question/math-academy-id "q-135325" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124616 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f53fa522-6d50-51d9-abdd-62735575a2d1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19e0631e-07fa-5259-8791-2c5926d4ae5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7}{10}" :db/id 17592186266359} {:answer/id #uuid "5686887c-bf1f-5eef-8d6c-4c47be372a18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{11}{13}" :db/id 17592186266913} {:answer/id #uuid "89d0ef52-9998-5e57-ac2e-1c6860957c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186267370} {:answer/id #uuid "8f0a0335-537e-50c2-9b17-5c27afb509f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186267419} {:answer/id #uuid "9726d41f-9c36-579a-af0e-92267c382c99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{13}" :db/id 17592186267496}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "9726d41f-9c36-579a-af0e-92267c382c99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{13}" :db/id 17592186267496} :answer-field/id #uuid "15f90970-79cf-5206-a259-f9ec67ec053f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186268442}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.3 \\ 1 & -0.3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+0.3{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 10{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{13}{10}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{10}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Car** | **Train** |
| To: | **Car** | $0.35$ | $0.25$ |
| **Train** | $0.65$ | $0.75$ |  |

It's found that $65%$ of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while $25%$ of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year.

Assuming that the town has $90\,000$ people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{18}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{18} \\ \frac{13}{18}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, $\frac{13}{18}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is

$$
\frac{13}{18}\cdot 90\,000=65\,000.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269057 :question/id #uuid "b9da89ba-6ad8-53a7-ac87-9c6b7aab9eb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-135409"} {:db/id 17592186411617 :question/id #uuid "fbc10db1-83ee-5f40-90d1-b581f73d6e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-135412" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d26e28b-a37c-5f8e-b505-641bddc3ac1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "82\,000" :db/id 17592186411598} {:answer/id #uuid "13e7a544-2b8e-535c-9dbd-150b4b2182d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "84\,000" :db/id 17592186411599} {:answer/id #uuid "62af4b1d-dead-5e6e-8055-bd94bce27217" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "65\,000" :db/id 17592186411605} {:answer/id #uuid "8d2be5c6-2ea1-5fdd-a19b-1ca6e9db49af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90\,000" :db/id 17592186411608} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0e3cc-f79a-5b7f-a8f4-e19e89af1d2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80\,000" :db/id 17592186411609}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411609} :answer-field/id #uuid "f22ac3a1-3b1b-5c02-9aac-e44227bf9c37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411614}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A study determines how customers' yearly preferences change between the LB and SB telephone companies. $$

$$

$$
{P}^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.187\,5 \\ 0.75 & 0.812\,5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 \\ 1 & -0.25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.25 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, $\frac{4}{5}$ of the customers will eventually use the SB company. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this company is

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 3 & -8 & 6.5 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -7.5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}+0.5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=\frac{1}{5}.

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -6 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & -14 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{14}{10}{x}_{3}=\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+2(\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{7}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{20}{5}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{7}{20} \\ \frac{1}{4}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{20}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269041 :question/id #uuid "7ff5c6dd-1891-5f28-95c5-0a779435ce27" :question/math-academy-id "q-135355"} {:db/id 17592186269059 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A study shows how the sports preferences of young people in a certain community vary from year to year. The following table shows the results of this study. 

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Baseball** | **Basketball** | **Football** |
| To: | **Baseball** | $0.8$ | $0.2$ | $0$ |
| **Basketball** | $0.1$ | $0.6$ | $0.2$ |  |
| **Football** | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ |  |

For example, $10%$ of people who used to prefer baseball now prefer football. 

Given that $1\,260$ young people were interviewed for the study and that the probabilities listed remain constant for many years, how many of those people will eventually prefer baseball?" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+0{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{3}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{3}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{2}{7}$ of the people will prefer baseball. Therefore, the number of people who will prefer baseball is

$$
\frac{2}{7}\cdot 1\,260=360\,\text{people}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186388820 :question/id #uuid "a031dbeb-978c-5542-b4e9-e4e60f2dc984" :question/math-academy-id "q-141024" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124617 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "84798595-cdd4-57bf-953f-0856b041b65f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aea59a55-ca8c-5011-94bb-adc5e2783f76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1\,360" :db/id 17592186388822} {:answer/id #uuid "8e324f12-a685-504b-be59-f46dd3f2728f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "340" :db/id 17592186388823} {:answer/id #uuid "02091894-fa17-5170-9a72-9c82ed0e6bbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "680" :db/id 17592186388824} {:answer/id #uuid "d0746dbd-50e5-51db-b5aa-9a4c741c97d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\,040" :db/id 17592186388825} {:answer/id #uuid "a69c66c2-72df-5f5b-aab3-269b3148afdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1\,700" :db/id 17592186388826}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a69c66c2-72df-5f5b-aab3-269b3148afdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1\,700" :db/id 17592186388826} :answer-field/id #uuid "c17d838d-64b9-5408-9e52-5f894639d0cb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186388821}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A study conducted on $3\,400$ teenagers by the transportation department of a particular city reveals that teenagers' preference for the type of home-to-school transportation changes with time. Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3})-{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{4}{10} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{1}{2}$ of the teenagers will go to school in electric scooters. Therefore, the total number of teenagers in the city that will go to school in electric scooters will be

$$
\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\,400=1\,700.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411615 :question/id #uuid "15361c81-aace-5a26-b7c5-2e82d38f451f" :question/math-academy-id "q-135349" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124617 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "84798595-cdd4-57bf-953f-0856b041b65f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09fa980f-8d16-5c0b-adc6-32aaa0351649" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186411597} {:answer/id #uuid "3f726a36-e309-5b98-8554-2e43c91e6dd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186411601} {:answer/id #uuid "47f65641-4908-5c8e-b21e-1a448edd51ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186411602} {:answer/id #uuid "49e05de2-77df-5db3-a385-91d68a9be627" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7}{9}" :db/id 17592186411603} {:answer/id #uuid "e6d1b46f-e211-5172-be37-ae8796943205" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186411610}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3f726a36-e309-5b98-8554-2e43c91e6dd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186411601} :answer-field/id #uuid "0e744f0f-1893-571c-a245-886e0be7796d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186411612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{3}-8{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}={x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e87c8124-0ff2-547b-8e5b-1dd24c33ff63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186459395} [{:db/id 17592186125565 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125849 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a stochastic matrix $P$ and a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}.$ Then, $\mathbf{q}$ is a **steady-state vector** of $P$ if 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

For example, to show that the stochastic vector 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

is a steady-state vector for the stochastic matrix 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

we compute the matrix product $P\mathbf q\mathbin:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0.94+2\cdot 0.03 \\ 0.06+2\cdot 0.97\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =q\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P\mathbf q = \mathbf q,$ the vector $\mathbf q$ is a steady-state vector of $P.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e1601d67-32bc-5796-a800-6e704f25f991" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5500 :tutorial/title "Steady-State Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "965fe16f-9c57-5058-9e32-90332314977c" :step/math-academy-id 34230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125566}} {:db/id 17592186125566 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124615 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124426 :question/id #uuid "8914449a-3d6f-5847-9e94-3be0a2ccbc94" :question/math-academy-id "e-9178"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f4f2f4f4-af4a-597d-b6c6-afb82e708fc2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049585} {:db/id 17592186050825}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124770} {:db/id 17592186124771} {:db/id 17592186269024} {:db/id 17592186269025} {:db/id 17592186269026} {:db/id 17592186269027} {:db/id 17592186411616}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "bd127c03-d025-5b21-ae93-e24b7aec916f" :step/math-academy-id 34231 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125567}} {:db/id 17592186125567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125850 :tutorial/content "To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute $(P-I):$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "78f635ff-e2e7-5c9f-9ec2-470187a45bc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5501 :tutorial/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix"} :step/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 34234} {:db/id 17592186125570 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125851 :tutorial/content "A stochastic matrix $P$ is **regular** if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P^n$ has all positive elements.

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

- The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
which has all positive elements. Therefore, $Q$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Regular stochastic matrices have the following important property:

> *Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
> $$
> 
> 
> converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and 

\[
P^n \mathbf{q}_0 \to \mathbf{q} 
\]

as [math]n \to \infty.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "255fadf0-9fc2-52d5-976b-015a97f52b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5502 :tutorial/title "Regular Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "735b7b96-43fa-5c0e-b4b8-df7598a6610b" :step/math-academy-id 34235 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125568}} {:db/id 17592186125588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{bmatrix} \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=\begin{bmatrix}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{bmatrix}\approx \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=\begin{bmatrix}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{bmatrix}\approx \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers." :tutorial/id #uuid "cb9435c4-44ed-58ec-9c04-b8fed4403fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6151 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7c429a3d-9dd8-5fe2-a7e7-cf0e9f515d1a" :step/math-academy-id 37332 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125565}}] :activity/title "Steady-State Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124712} {:db/id 17592186125588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. $$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute $(P-I):$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "78f635ff-e2e7-5c9f-9ec2-470187a45bc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5501 :tutorial/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "429ea8df-33bc-5c79-a0d6-97b71166cd98" :step/math-academy-id 34232 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125570}} {:db/id 17592186125850 :tutorial/content "To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

Finally, our steady-state vector is

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "78f635ff-e2e7-5c9f-9ec2-470187a45bc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5501 :tutorial/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186125570 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125851 :tutorial/content "A stochastic matrix $P$ is **regular** if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P^n$ has all positive elements.

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

- The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
which has all positive elements. Therefore, $Q$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Regular stochastic matrices have the following important property:

> *Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
> $$
> 
> 
> converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and 

\[
P^n \mathbf{q}_0 \to \mathbf{q} 
\]

as [math]n \to \infty.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "255fadf0-9fc2-52d5-976b-015a97f52b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5502 :tutorial/title "Regular Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid - The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by

contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get

\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}

which has all positive elements. Therefore, $Q$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Regular stochastic matrices have the following important property:

> *Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
> $$
> 
> 
> converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and 

\[

\]

as [math]n \to \infty.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "255fadf0-9fc2-52d5-976b-015a97f52b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5502 :tutorial/title "Regular Stochastic Matrices"} {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{bmatrix} \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=\begin{bmatrix}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{bmatrix}\approx \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=\begin{bmatrix}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{bmatrix}\approx \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers." :tutorial/id #uuid "cb9435c4-44ed-58ec-9c04-b8fed4403fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6151 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046673} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186411620} :activity/id #uuid "86878afe-0434-571a-8f3d-da4de43c4751" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048393 :topic/id #uuid "9babae1d-ca0d-5438-a2e4-a65dbba9f7ef" :topic/math-academy-id 1913} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186411618 :step/content {:db/id 17592186411615 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09fa980f-8d16-5c0b-adc6-32aaa0351649" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186411597} {:answer/id #uuid "3f726a36-e309-5b98-8554-2e43c91e6dd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186411601} {:answer/id #uuid "47f65641-4908-5c8e-b21e-1a448edd51ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186411602} {:answer/id #uuid "49e05de2-77df-5db3-a385-91d68a9be627" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{9}" :db/id 17592186411603} {:answer/id #uuid "e6d1b46f-e211-5172-be37-ae8796943205" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186411610}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411601} :answer-field/id #uuid "0e744f0f-1893-571c-a245-886e0be7796d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "15361c81-aace-5a26-b7c5-2e82d38f451f" :question/math-academy-id "q-135349" :question/problem "$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{3}-8{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}={x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, note that

$$
{P}^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.187\,5 \\ 0.75 & 0.812\,5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 \\ 1 & -0.25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.25 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, $\frac{4}{5}$ of the customers will eventually use the SB company. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this company is

$$
\frac{4}{5}\cdot 100\,000=80\,000.
