:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167943 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168034 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will represent a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ as an infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the **Fourier series** for $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

The key idea is that we can "build" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.

![](images/39/392a8df0fab00010e76036aa0fec2c60f25b5766b3cacc7983b7443d909866eb.png)

This gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.

To work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as $[-\pi,\pi),$ and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a **periodic extension**.

In the next slide, we will define this concept formally and look at some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d19e02d-99c0-5649-b7a3-bdb37c8e97e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14624 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "822d573c-a967-52e4-854c-d2b5f14b0fff" :step/math-academy-id 600573 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167955}} {:db/id 17592186167944 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166562 :question/id #uuid "5888d4ce-bc45-540b-afa0-901008abfcde" :question/math-academy-id "e-21787"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049091} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167264} {:db/id 17592186167265} {:db/id 17592186311951} {:db/id 17592186314968} {:db/id 17592186315068} {:db/id 17592186315069} {:db/id 17592186413394} {:db/id 17592186413395} {:db/id 17592186548057} {:db/id 17592186554574}] :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c6f0ea8f-2008-5f49-84d9-7341157766fc" :step/math-academy-id 600574 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167945}} {:db/id 17592186167945 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Also recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=0.$

The key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions

$$
1,\ \cos(x),\ \sin(x),\ \cos(2x),\ \sin(2x),\ \ldots
$$

are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.

More precisely, for integers $m,n\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

- $\langle \cos(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$

- $\langle \sin(mx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$ and

- $\langle \sin(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$

Also, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:

- $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ and

- $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Finally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:

$$
\langle 1,1\rangle=2\pi,
\quad
\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\pi
\quad
\text{for all } n\ge 1.
$$

Let's see how this works in concrete examples.

**Note:** Both intervals $[-\pi,\pi)$ and $[0,2\pi)$ are considered standard in this context. We’ll use $[-\pi,\pi)$ in tutorials, but some exercises use $[0,2\pi).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9c1c7f37-624c-5c49-9ded-2b3dd3b37d7a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14639 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Orthogonal Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f80997bd-d9ed-5a35-b485-c34868575480" :step/math-academy-id 600578 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167946}} {:db/id 17592186167946 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166963 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166563 :question/id #uuid "052f11a0-2f27-5285-83af-6d8fdb729024" :question/math-academy-id "e-21788"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fadf4f64-3569-56b2-98e1-f6681892054a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049303} {:db/id 17592186049850} {:db/id 17592186050331}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167274} {:db/id 17592186167275} {:db/id 17592186314939} {:db/id 17592186314940} {:db/id 17592186314970} {:db/id 17592186314993} {:db/id 17592186314994} {:db/id 17592186314995} {:db/id 17592186314996} {:db/id 17592186315084} {:db/id 17592186397472} {:db/id 17592186413393} {:db/id 17592186526085}] :knowledge-point/title "Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines"} :step/id #uuid "b4a0ba44-f514-5920-a47f-39a8f107bb7d" :step/math-academy-id 600579 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167947}} {:db/id 17592186167947 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168035 :tutorial/content "Recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We can represent $f(x)$ by its Fourier series:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients $a_0, a_n,$ and $b_n.$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} :step/id #uuid "769e9784-6852-5663-879d-f2dd13159e0a" :step/math-academy-id 600583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167956}} {:db/id 17592186167948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166964 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166564 :question/id #uuid "d2127a8e-14bb-5574-a542-852333fe4cca" :question/math-academy-id "e-21789"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "304c015d-cbb6-5989-a102-d6f0f5f38604" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048169} {:db/id 17592186050841}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167282} {:db/id 17592186167291} {:db/id 17592186314985} {:db/id 17592186314987} {:db/id 17592186314988} {:db/id 17592186314989} {:db/id 17592186314991} {:db/id 17592186315082} {:db/id 17592186397418} {:db/id 17592186397438} {:db/id 17592186397539} {:db/id 17592186547996} {:db/id 17592186548063}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Expressions For Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "52c506ad-0e1c-5f71-b513-284e3650dd10" :step/math-academy-id 600584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167949}} {:db/id 17592186167949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

To determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the lesson.

Now, we derive the formula for $a_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\cos(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\cos(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle=a_n\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
a_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, we derive the formula for $b_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\sin(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "4fc54380-13dd-5632-a907-a555a9ed5733" :step/math-academy-id 600587} {:db/id 17592186167955 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168052 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *$p$-periodic* if $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$  

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} :step/id #uuid "c98bd153-6ef6-5953-a668-095e59197be9" :step/math-academy-id 606168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167944}} {:db/id 17592186167956 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :tutorial/title "The Formula For the Constant Term"} :step/id #uuid "a0bab88b-45ac-5613-b8cf-64b1eafabee1" :step/math-academy-id 606214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167948}}] :activity/title "Introduction to Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166990} {:db/id 17592186167943 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168034 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will represent a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ as an infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the **Fourier series** for $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

The key idea is that we can "build" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.

![](images/39/392a8df0fab00010e76036aa0fec2c60f25b5766b3cacc7983b7443d909866eb.png)

This gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.

To work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as $[-\pi,\pi),$ and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a **periodic extension**.

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} :step/id #uuid "c98bd153-6ef6-5953-a668-095e59197be9" :step/math-academy-id 606168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167944}} {:db/id 17592186167944 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166562 :question/id #uuid "5888d4ce-bc45-540b-afa0-901008abfcde" :question/math-academy-id "e-21787"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049091} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167264} {:db/id 17592186167265} {:db/id 17592186311951} {:db/id 17592186314968} {:db/id 17592186315068} {:db/id 17592186315069} {:db/id 17592186413394} {:db/id 17592186413395} {:db/id 17592186548057} {:db/id 17592186554574}] :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c6f0ea8f-2008-5f49-84d9-7341157766fc" :step/math-academy-id 600574 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167945}} {:db/id 17592186167945 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Also recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=0.$

The key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions

$$
1,\ \cos(x),\ \sin(x),\ \cos(2x),\ \sin(2x),\ \ldots
$$

are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.

More precisely, for integers $m,n\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

- $\langle \cos(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$

- $\langle \sin(mx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$ and

- $\langle \sin(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$

Also, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:

- $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ and

- $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Finally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:

$$
\langle 1,1\rangle=2\pi,
\quad
\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\pi
\quad
\text{for all } n\ge 1.
$$

Let's see how this works in concrete examples.

**Note:** Both intervals $[-\pi,\pi)$ and $[0,2\pi)$ are considered standard in this context. We’ll use $[-\pi,\pi)$ in tutorials, but some exercises use $[0,2\pi).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9c1c7f37-624c-5c49-9ded-2b3dd3b37d7a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14639 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Orthogonal Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f80997bd-d9ed-5a35-b485-c34868575480" :step/math-academy-id 600578 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167946}} {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients $a_0, a_n,$ and $b_n.$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} :step/id #uuid "769e9784-6852-5663-879d-f2dd13159e0a" :step/math-academy-id 600583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167956}} {:db/id 17592186168035 :tutorial/content "Recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We can represent $f(x)$ by its Fourier series:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} {:db/id 17592186167956 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :tutorial/title "The Formula For the Constant Term"} :step/id #uuid "a0bab88b-45ac-5613-b8cf-64b1eafabee1" :step/math-academy-id 606214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167948}} {:db/id 17592186167948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166964 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166564 :question/id #uuid "d2127a8e-14bb-5574-a542-852333fe4cca" :question/math-academy-id "e-21789"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "304c015d-cbb6-5989-a102-d6f0f5f38604" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048169} {:db/id 17592186050841}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167282} {:db/id 17592186167291} {:db/id 17592186314985} {:db/id 17592186314987} {:db/id 17592186314988} {:db/id 17592186314989} {:db/id 17592186314991} {:db/id 17592186315082} {:db/id 17592186397418} {:db/id 17592186397438} {:db/id 17592186397539} {:db/id 17592186547996} {:db/id 17592186548063}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Expressions For Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "52c506ad-0e1c-5f71-b513-284e3650dd10" :step/math-academy-id 600584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167949}} {:db/id 17592186167949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

To determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the lesson.

Now, we derive the formula for $a_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\cos(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\cos(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle=a_n\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
a_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, we derive the formula for $b_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\sin(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "4fc54380-13dd-5632-a907-a555a9ed5733" :step/math-academy-id 600587} {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} {:db/id 17592186168052 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *$p$-periodic* if $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$  

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 "0dea1a3b-78f2-5704-9965-e3fb9de63bfa" :question/math-academy-id "q-340647" :question/problem "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi ))) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7db2bec7-56bf-57ee-b02e-da70da5a3acc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526130}} {:db/id 17592186526130 :step/content {:db/id 17592186314991 :question/answer-fields "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-6x$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{4}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(16\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩} \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({x}^{2}-6x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8d83434b-1efb-5984-8cbe-1830c4537f9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526142}} {:db/id 17592186526142 :step/content {:db/id 17592186526085 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b761040-6bc5-5857-9c79-db2a13d27611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "are not orthogonal" :db/id 17592186525349} {:answer/id #uuid "edaa6194-fdee-5a52-85e0-2ed9f495bf4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "are orthogonal" :db/id 17592186525797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186525797} :answer-field/id #uuid "55543445-1727-5019-a16d-94fb1228f51e" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186525890} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c5912f1-7503-5114-bd94-c09318d2aa64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186525231} {:answer/id #uuid "bf39a84a-5b39-5bb5-8f67-5b65a043baf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186525695} {:answer/id #uuid "ed84a8fc-5d46-52dc-beb9-dfab6973e8cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186525796} {:answer/id #uuid "fea342fe-4c4d-5c10-87ec-9f65ac0a4202" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186525840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186525840} :answer-field/id #uuid "f22a4739-c628-52a9-ae16-699a277e6c24" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186525971}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d85f2141-c945-5a8d-a74b-f86923a41441" :question/math-academy-id "q-340668" :question/problem "$$

"0dea1a3b-78f2-5704-9965-e3fb9de63bfa" :question/math-academy-id "q-340647" :question/problem "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi ))) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7db2bec7-56bf-57ee-b02e-da70da5a3acc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526130}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08fed8a6-dde9-59a6-bc31-184c4876910c" :answer/type {:db/id $$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{4}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(16\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩} \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({x}^{2}-6x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$f(x)=6x^4-7x^3+11x-9,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-9,$ and its factors are $\pm1,$ $\pm3,$ and $\pm9.$

- The leading coefficient is $6,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2,$ $\pm 3,$ and $\pm 6.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm \frac{3}{3}, & \pm \frac{3}{6}, \\ \pm \frac{9}{1}, & \pm \frac{9}{2}, & \pm \frac{9}{3}, & \pm \frac{9}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, \\ \pm 9, & \pm \frac{9}{2}, & \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that several potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{6}, \; \pm \frac13, \; \pm \frac12, \; \pm 1, \; \pm \frac32, \; \pm 3, \; \pm \frac{9}{2}, \; \pm 9.
$$

This makes a total of $16$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm$ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2 \cdot 8 = 16.$)"} {:db/id 17592186083535 :question/id #uuid "aeb1ad5f-0910-5dea-b64a-e03889cc2cc5" :question/math-academy-id "q-14145"} {:db/id 17592186083536 :question/id #uuid "df06ddf2-698f-54af-b10e-2e279114c1c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-14147"} {:db/id 17592186233456 :question/id #uuid "66ae1650-566a-5bce-8d4c-8b63d98b0a02" :question/math-academy-id "q-14140" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "273c6dd0-67fe-528d-98c1-8dad19a58e5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186436911} {:answer/id #uuid "4a0177fe-6f1f-5c81-84de-6277949370ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186436912} {:answer/id #uuid "8a571250-310b-5aff-b6f3-4de1c0dc69f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186436913} {:answer/id #uuid "ad17155f-b4cd-54ec-8be4-28ea64a81659" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186436914} {:answer/id #uuid "b2275ff8-fe98-5084-bd82-ea5aaba7e949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186436915}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436912} :answer-field/id #uuid "6eafbdc9-1f3b-58eb-b092-b6276d35ea08" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436916}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "For the polynomial $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-x+12,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.

- The constant term is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm 6, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm \frac{2}{5},\,\pm \frac{3}{5},\,\pm \frac{4}{5},\,\pm 1\,\pm \frac{6}{5},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{12}{5},\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 12.
$$

This makes a total of $24$ potential roots. rational roots theorem?" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $4,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2$ and $\pm 4.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{2}, & \pm \frac{2}{4}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm \frac{3}{4}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{2}, & \pm \frac{4}{4}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{2}, & \pm \frac{6}{4}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{2}, & \pm \frac{12}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm \frac{3}{4}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm 2, & \pm 1, \\ \pm 6, & \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm 6, & \pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{4},\,\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm \frac{3}{4},\,\pm 1,\,\pm \frac{3}{2},\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 12.
$$

This makes a total of $20$ potential roots. $$

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm \frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $4$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of }{4}}{\textrm{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm1, \pm 2, \pm 4
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,4),$ are $1$ and $2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $\left(x-1\right)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-4$ | $4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-4$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $-4$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $\left(x-1\right)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x) = \left( x - 1\right) (x^2 - 4).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-1)({x}^{2}-4) \\  & =(x-1)(x+2)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-25$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-25}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 25,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{5}{3},\,\pm \frac{25}{3}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ are $-1$ and $-\frac{5}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{5}{3}$ | $3$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $25$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-15$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{5}{3},-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{5}{3}-\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186083682 :question/id #uuid "e7bd90fd-0fb1-553e-84d3-ad65f76b3093" :question/math-academy-id "q-39038"} {:db/id 17592186233828 :question/id #uuid $$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-21$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-21}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 7,\,\pm 21,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{7}{3}.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(-3,-2)$ is $-\frac{7}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{7}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{7}{3}$ | $3$ | $7$ | $-9$ | $-21$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-7$ | $0$ | $21$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-9$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{7}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{7}{3})(3{x}^{2}-9).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{7}{3})(3{x}^{2}-9) \\  & =3(x+\frac{7}{3})({x}^{2}-3) \\  & =3(x+\frac{7}{3})(x+\sqrt{3})(x-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find that, in ascending order, the roots of the polynomial are $x=-\frac{7}{3},$ $x=-\sqrt{3},$ and $x=\sqrt{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186326676 :question/id #uuid $$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-6$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-6}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm \frac{3}{2},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 6
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $2$ | $9$ | $7$ | $-6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $5$ | $6$ |
|  | $2$ | $10$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-\frac{1}{2})(2{x}^{2}+10x+12).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{1}{2})(2{x}^{2}+10x+12) \\  & =2(x-\frac{1}{2})({x}^{2}+5x+6) \\  & =2(x-\frac{1}{2})(x+2)(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=\frac{1}{2},-2,-3.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
\frac{1}{2}-2-3=-\frac{9}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186433675 :question/id #uuid "b9c7c178-4ebe-5318-8cb7-742204e595a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-112977"} {:db/id 17592186492830 :question/id #uuid "12d33f18-863a-5b25-ace7-f97482164c70" :question/math-academy-id "q-323572" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d17d593-2ae4-53d7-a4b5-82e61d1bfa57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186492236}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186492236} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1ef24a4-cbc2-5e7b-841f-6bdc135e149a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186492791}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-x-15$ has a root in the interval $(1,4),$ the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x)$ equals{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

:topic/math-academy-id 757} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084136 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084456 :tutorial/content "The **rational roots theorem** (or **rational zeros theorem**) describes the rational roots of a polynomial with integer coefficients. The statement of the theorem is as follows:

*Suppose that the rational number $\dfrac{{\color{blue}{p}}}{\color{red}{q}},$ in lowest terms, is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients. Then $\color{blue}p$ must be a factor of the polynomial's constant term, and $\color{red}q$ must be a factor of its leading coefficient.*

In other words, given a polynomial with integer coefficients, any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(x) = {\color{red}{8}}x^3+12x^2+6x+{\color{blue}{2}}.
$$

According to the rational roots theorem, any rational root of $f(x)$ must have a numerator that is a factor of $\color{blue}{2}$ (that is, either $\color{blue} \pm1$ or $\color{blue} \pm2$) and a denominator that's a factor of $\color{red} 8$ (${\color{red} \pm1},$ ${\color{red} \pm2},$ ${\color{red} \pm4},$ or $\color{red} \pm8$). 

At first glance, it may seem like we have $16$ possible rational roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{8}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{2}, & \pm \frac{2}{4}, & \pm \frac{2}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

However, if we reduce the above fractions to lowest form, we see that there are some duplicates, which we cancel out:

![](images/91/91d3a123202f03ecec2d568548b5964fdc941e77d9edbad8ab386954bb046740.svg) 

Removing the duplicates, we have ten *possible* rational roots. We list them from least to greatest in absolute value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{8}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm 1, & \pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Watch out!** The above roots are only *possible* rational roots. They are *not* guaranteed to be roots of our polynomial $f(x).$ The only guarantee is that if $f(x)$ has any roots that are rational numbers, they are included in the list of numbers above. Here, it turns out that the only actual root among the possibilities is $-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "85dfd162-8cfc-59dd-8f7d-d66bbde1873c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3729 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :tutorial/content "The **rational roots theorem** (or **rational zeros theorem**) describes the rational roots of a polynomial with integer coefficients. The statement of the theorem is as follows:

*Suppose that the rational number $\dfrac{{\color{blue}{p}}}{\color{red}{q}},$ in lowest terms, is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients. Then $\color{blue}p$ must be a factor of the polynomial's constant term, and $\color{red}q$ must be a factor of its leading coefficient.*

In other words, given a polynomial with integer coefficients, any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(x) = {\color{red}{8}}x^3+12x^2+6x+{\color{blue}{2}}.
$$

According to the rational roots theorem, any rational root of $f(x)$ must have a numerator that is a factor of $\color{blue}{2}$ (that is, either $\color{blue} \pm1$ or $\color{blue} \pm2$) and a denominator that's a factor of $\color{red} 8$ (${\color{red} \pm1},$ ${\color{red} \pm2},$ ${\color{red} \pm4},$ or $\color{red} \pm8$). 

At first glance, it may seem like we have $16$ possible rational roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{8}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{2}, & \pm \frac{2}{4}, & \pm \frac{2}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

However, if we reduce the above fractions to lowest form, we see that there are some duplicates, which we cancel out:

![](images/91/91d3a123202f03ecec2d568548b5964fdc941e77d9edbad8ab386954bb046740.svg) 

Removing the duplicates, we have ten *possible* rational roots. We list them from least to greatest in absolute value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{8}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm 1, & \pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Watch out!** The above roots are only *possible* rational roots. They are *not* guaranteed to be roots of our polynomial $f(x).$ The only guarantee is that if $f(x)$ has any roots that are rational numbers, they are included in the list of numbers above. Here, it turns out that the only actual root among the possibilities is $-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "85dfd162-8cfc-59dd-8f7d-d66bbde1873c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3729 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5b104caf-8c0c-5010-8dfa-bbe8604d3403" :step/math-academy-id 20965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084241}} {:db/id 17592186084456 :tutorial/content "The **rational roots theorem** (or **rational zeros theorem**) describes the rational roots of a polynomial with integer coefficients. $$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm 6, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm \frac{2}{5},\,\pm \frac{3}{5},\,\pm \frac{4}{5},\,\pm 1\,\pm \frac{6}{5},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{12}{5},\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 12.
$$

This makes a total of $24$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 12=24.$)"} :step/id #uuid "74fc6fe2-50c7-5458-827e-99d2e1df0a79" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436919}} {:db/id 17592186436919 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083681 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "135f42a4-d1ee-5f2c-af3a-0c8aa0176bf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186324143} {:answer/id #uuid "268df909-c8fb-563f-af2f-c08134584f25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186324283} {:answer/id #uuid "69e770f2-5fac-5581-b92a-b1b948231e35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186324857} {:answer/id #uuid "8b3c6363-b72d-5a0d-9eec-918fa9888a08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186325152} {:answer/id #uuid "fc9d3f67-6d9d-5067-8456-4fe529f4d545" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186326194}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324857} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f2953d1-fb0d-5e3e-8ec9-21bd1672c52d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f572c08e-edf8-5f9d-9827-c106bc98ece4" :question/math-academy-id "q-39033" :question/problem "Given that the polynomial $f(x)=3{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}-15x-25$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-25$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-25}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 25,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{5}{3},\,\pm \frac{25}{3}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ are $-1$ and $-\frac{5}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{5}{3}$ | $3$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $25$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-15$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{5}{3},-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{5}{3}-\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}.

$f(x)=3{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}-15x-25$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-25$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-25}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 25,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{5}{3},\,\pm \frac{25}{3}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ are $-1$ and $-\frac{5}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{5}{3}$ | $3$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $25$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-15$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{5}{3},-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{5}{3}-\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7ff2104b-6a5b-5774-95cc-77db99183716" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436917}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "135f42a4-d1ee-5f2c-af3a-0c8aa0176bf9" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $1,$ and its factors are $\pm 1.$

- The leading coefficient is $4,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2$ and $\pm 4.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This makes a total of $6$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 3=6.$)"} :step/id #uuid "58d4a216-d386-5004-acc6-1259a07e1494" :step/next {:db/id 17592186509011}} {:db/id 17592186509023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186302137 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b16f84b-0fdd-5a3e-8aa0-dc62596d443c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186300664}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300664} :answer-field/id #uuid "410552d6-05ce-5fcd-88f6-0b3a368b5a06" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186301446}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "fd8abfc9-fc42-5fbe-8914-ffe40a38eb8b" :question/math-academy-id "q-323218" :question/problem "According to the rational root theorem, the polynomial $f(x)=7{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-7$ has{{field-1}} *potential* rational roots." :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$

- The leading coefficient is $7,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 7.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{7}, \\ \pm \frac{7}{1}, & \pm \frac{7}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$

$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

 {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-21$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-21}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 7,\,\pm 21,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{7}{3}.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(-3,-2)$ is $-\frac{7}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{7}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{7}{3}$ | $3$ | $7$ | $-9$ | $-21$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-7$ | $0$ | $21$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-9$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{7}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{7}{3})(3{x}^{2}-9).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{7}{3})(3{x}^{2}-9) \\  & =3(x+\frac{7}{3})({x}^{2}-3) \\  & =3(x+\frac{7}{3})(x+\sqrt{3})(x-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find that, in ascending order, the roots of the polynomial are $x=-\frac{7}{3},$ $x=-\sqrt{3},$ and $x=\sqrt{3}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c5006e3f-438a-526e-aab3-e8ec1d08a5ad"} {:db/id 17592186509041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186492830 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d17d593-2ae4-53d7-a4b5-82e61d1bfa57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186492236}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186492236} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1ef24a4-cbc2-5e7b-841f-6bdc135e149a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186492791}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "12d33f18-863a-5b25-ace7-f97482164c70" :question/math-academy-id "q-323572" :question/problem "Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-x-15$ has a root in the interval $(1,4),$ the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x)$ equals{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }15}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 15.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(1,4)$ is $3.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $6$ | $15$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $5$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-3)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-3)({x}^{2}+2x+5).
$$

Now we must see if the polynomial $g(x)={x}^{2}+2x+5$ has real roots. For this, we must find the value of its discriminant $D.$ Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={2}^{2}-4(1)(5) \\  & =4-20 \\  & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D<0,$ the polynomial $g(x)$ doesn't have real roots.

$$

- The constant term is $-7,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 7.$

- The leading coefficient is $7,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 7.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{7}, \\ \pm \frac{7}{1}, & \pm \frac{7}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{7}, \\ \pm 7, & \pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{7},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 7.
$$

This makes a total of $6$ potential roots. $$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-15$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }15}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 15.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(1,4)$ is $3.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-15$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $6$ | $15$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $5$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-3)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-3)({x}^{2}+2x+5).
$$

Now we must see if the polynomial $g(x)={x}^{2}+2x+5$ has real roots. For this, we must find the value of its discriminant $D.$ Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={2}^{2}-4(1)(5) \\  & =4-20 \\  & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D<0,$ the polynomial $g(x)$ doesn't have real roots.

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

|  | $↓$ | $-7$ | $0$ | $21$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-9$ | $0$ |

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{7}{3})(3{x}^{2}-9).
$$

$$

- The first operation is ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operation is ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$
