$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Then, to apply the second elementary row operation to ${E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{2}$ on the left and get ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$"} {:db/id 17592186302071 :question/id #uuid "4d615245-8860-57bd-9182-e8271d3465f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-32148"} {:db/id 17592186329663 :question/id #uuid What is the equivalent notation in terms of matrix multiplication?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the elementary matrices corresponding to the given elementary row operations.

- The first operation is ${R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operation is ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operation is ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To apply the first elementary row operation to the matrix $A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{1}$ on the left and get ${E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Then, to apply the second elementary row operation to ${E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{2}$ on the left and get ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Finally, to apply the third elementary row operation to ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{3}$ on the left and get ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

"q-110493" :question/problem "Suppose that the following elementary row operations are applied to a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ in the given order:

$$
{R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}
$$

What is the equivalent notation in terms of matrix multiplication?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the elementary matrices corresponding to the given elementary row operations.

- The first operation is ${R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operation is ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operation is ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To apply the first elementary row operation to the matrix $A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{1}$ on the left and get ${E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Then, to apply the second elementary row operation to ${E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{2}$ on the left and get ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Finally, to apply the third elementary row operation to ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{3}$ on the left and get ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$ 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equivalent notation in terms of matrix multiplication is $EA:$

- The first operation is ${R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operation is ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operation is ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={E}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To apply the first elementary row operation to the matrix $A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{1}$ on the left and get ${E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Then, to apply the second elementary row operation to ${E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{2}$ on the left and get ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot A
$$

Finally, to apply the third elementary row operation to ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{3}$ on the left and get ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$ 

$$

For which of the following transformations can the change-of-variables method be applied to find the probability density function of $Y$?

1. $Y = X^4$, where $X\in (0,2)$
2. $Y = \cos X$, where $X\in (-\infty, \infty)$
3. $Y = e^{-X}$, where $X\in (0, \infty)$" :question/worked-solution "The change-of-variables method can be applied when a transformation $Y = u(X)$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing (i.e., strictly monotonic) over the entire support of $X$.

With that in mind, let's inspect each transformation in turn.

- Transformation I is strictly monotonic. The function $u(x) = x^4$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (0,2)$.
- Transformation II is *not* strictly monotonic. For example, $u(x) = \cos x$ is decreasing on $x \in \left(0,\pi \right)$ and increasing on $x \in \left(\pi,2\pi\right)$.
- Transformation III is strictly monotonic. The function $u(x) =e^{-x}$ is strictly decreasing for $x\in (0,\infty)$.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186049573} {:db/id 17592186162259 :question/id #uuid "9e9d5f0f-2ef7-529c-8fdb-10e2c56f1d5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-108883"} {:db/id 17592186162278 :question/id #uuid "f7437682-9b5e-5b3d-9686-8ab0f51fd6da" :question/math-academy-id "q-109175"} {:db/id 17592186162053 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161853 :question/id #uuid "2fd76ea7-ab08-5afa-9762-158a85999321" :question/math-academy-id "e-9101"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "26854b8e-68bc-5e69-8fcd-fa46b72d05c3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049956} {:db/id 17592186050322}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162260 :question/id #uuid "852c5bdf-27f0-59e5-9788-1be0252ab091" :question/math-academy-id "q-108884"} {:db/id 17592186162399 :question/id #uuid "b74848bf-6333-5417-a2d8-415863aeaf3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-143762"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the PDF of a Random Variable Under an Affine Transformation"} {:db/id 17592186161853 :question/id #uuid "2fd76ea7-ab08-5afa-9762-158a85999321" :question/math-academy-id "e-9101" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186162053 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "26854b8e-68bc-5e69-8fcd-fa46b72d05c3" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the PDF of a Random Variable Under an Affine Transformation"}] :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

If $Y = \dfrac{1-X}{4}$, use the change-of-variables method to find the probability density function of $Y$." :question/worked-solution "If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f_X$ and $Y = u(X)$, where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by
${f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot\begin{vmatrix}(u^{-1})^{′}(y) &,\end{vmatrix}yis betweenu(a)andu(b); 0, \mid otherwise$.

The transformation

$$
u(x) = \dfrac{1-x}{4}
$$

is strictly monotonically *decreasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find $u^{-1}(y)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u(y) &= \frac{1 - y}{4} \\
y &= (1 - u^{-1}(y))/(4) \\
u^{-1}(y) &= 1 - 4y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $(u^{-1})'(y){:}$

$$
(u^{-1})'(y) = -4
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero $f_Y$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot \mid (u^{-1})^{′}(y) \mid \\

&= \frac{1}{156}(1 - 4y)^{3} \cdot 4 \\
&= \frac{1}{39}(1 - 4y)^{3}
\end{aligned}

:tutorial/content "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is known. We know that if $Y = u(X)$, then we can apply the distribution function method to compute the PDF of $Y$.

It's possible to generalize the distribution function method when $u(X)$ is strictly monotonic. This generalization is known as the **change-of-variables method**, and is stated below:

> *If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f_X$ and $Y = u(X)$, where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by*
> ${f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot\begin{vmatrix}(u^{-1})^{′}(y) &,\end{vmatrix}yis betweenu(a)andu(b); 0, \mid otherwise$.

Proof of this result will be provided at the end of the lesson.

The advantage of the change-of-variables method is that it's often easier and faster to implement than the distribution function method. The disadvantage is that it only works when $u$ is monotonic, whereas the distribution function method can be extended to deal with non-monotonic functions.

For example, suppose that $X$ has the probability density function

$$
{\frac{1}{2}x,\begin{vmatrix}0 < x < 2 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Let the random variable $Y = 3X$. Then $u(x) = 3x$, which is strictly monotonically increasing. Therefore, the change-of-variables method can be used to compute the PDF of $Y$.

First, we find $u^{-1}(y)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u(y) &= 3y \\
y &= 3u^{-1}(y) \\
u^{-1}(y) &= \frac{1}{3}y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $(u^{-1})'(y){:}$

$$
u^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{1}{3}y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (u^{-1})'(y) = \dfrac{1}{3}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero $f_Y$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot \mid (u^{-1})^{′}(y) \mid \\
&= f_{X}(\frac{1}{3}y) \cdot \mid \frac{1}{3} \mid \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}y) \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\
&= \frac{1}{18}y
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $f_X$ is nonzero on $0 < x < 2$, the bounds are $a=0$ and $b=2$, and we have

$$
u(0) = 0, \qquad u(2) = 6
$$

Therefore, the probability distribution of $Y$ is

$$
{\frac{1}{18}y,\begin{vmatrix}0 < y < 6 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86b37435-f432-5855-9152-51435d0e102c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5356 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4d93e146-01aa-543e-9cbb-e868641f90cd" :step/math-academy-id change-of-variables method:

> *If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f_X$ and $Y = u(X)$, where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by*
> ${f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot\begin{vmatrix}(u^{-1})^{′}(y) &,\end{vmatrix}yis betweenu(a)andu(b); 0, \mid otherwise$.

Now, let's prove this result.

The first part is simple. Because $X$ is between $a$ and $b$, and $u$ is monotonic, $Y=u(X)$ must be between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$. So

$$
f_Y(y) = 0
$$

when $y$ is not between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$.

To carry out the rest of the proof, we will need to apply the distribution function method in two cases:

- **Case 1**: $u$ is monotonically increasing
- **Case 2**: $u$ is monotonically decreasing

We'll consider the case where $u$ is monotonically increasing only. The proof when $u$ is monotonically decreasing is similar.

First, we find the cumulative distribution of $Y$. Assuming $y$ is between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{Y}(y) &= P(Y \le y) \\
&= P(u(X) \le y) \\
&= P(X \le u^{-1}(y)) \\
&= \int_{a}^{u^{-1}(y)}f_{X}(t)dt \\
&= \left.F_{X}(t)\right|_{a}^{u^{-1}(y)} \\
&= F_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) - F_{X}(a)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we differentiate to get the probability density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= \frac{d}{dy}[F_{Y}(y)] \\
&= \frac{d}{dy}[F_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) - F_{X}(a)] \\
&= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y))(u^{-1})^{′}(y)
\end{aligned}
$$

It's possible to generalize the distribution function method when $u(X)$ is strictly monotonic. This generalization is known as the **change-of-variables method**, and is stated below:

> *If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f_X$ and $Y = u(X)$, where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by*
> ${f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot\begin{vmatrix}(u^{-1})^{′}(y) &,\end{vmatrix}yis betweenu(a)andu(b); 0, \mid otherwise$.

Proof of this result will be provided at the end of the lesson.

The advantage of the change-of-variables method is that it's often easier and faster to implement than the distribution function method. The disadvantage is that it only works when $u$ is monotonic, whereas the distribution function method can be extended to deal with non-monotonic functions.

For example, suppose that $X$ has the probability density function

$$
{\frac{1}{2}x,\begin{vmatrix}0 < x < 2 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Let the random variable $Y = 3X$. Then $u(x) = 3x$, which is strictly monotonically increasing. Therefore, the change-of-variables method can be used to compute the PDF of $Y$.

First, we find $u^{-1}(y)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u(y) &= 3y \\
y &= 3u^{-1}(y) \\
u^{-1}(y) &= \frac{1}{3}y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $(u^{-1})'(y){:}$

$$
u^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{1}{3}y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (u^{-1})'(y) = \dfrac{1}{3}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero $f_Y$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot \mid (u^{-1})^{′}(y) \mid \\
&= f_{X}(\frac{1}{3}y) \cdot \mid \frac{1}{3} \mid \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}y) \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\
&= \frac{1}{18}y
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $f_X$ is nonzero on $0 < x < 2$, the bounds are $a=0$ and $b=2$, and we have

$$
u(0) = 0, \qquad u(2) = 6
$$

Therefore, the probability distribution of $Y$ is

$$
{\frac{1}{18}y,\begin{vmatrix}0 < y < 6 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86b37435-f432-5855-9152-51435d0e102c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5356 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4d93e146-01aa-543e-9cbb-e868641f90cd" :step/math-academy-id 33486 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162966}} {:db/id 17592186163264 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is known. > *If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f_X$ and $Y = u(X)$, where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by*
> ${f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \cdot\begin{vmatrix}(u^{-1})^{′}(y) &,\end{vmatrix}yis betweenu(a)andu(b); 0, \mid otherwise$.

Now, let's prove this result.

The first part is simple. Because $X$ is between $a$ and $b$, and $u$ is monotonic, $Y=u(X)$ must be between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$. So

$$
f_Y(y) = 0
$$

when $y$ is not between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$.

To carry out the rest of the proof, we will need to apply the distribution function method in two cases:

- **Case 1**: $u$ is monotonically increasing
- **Case 2**: $u$ is monotonically decreasing

We'll consider the case where $u$ is monotonically increasing only. The proof when $u$ is monotonically decreasing is similar.

First, we find the cumulative distribution of $Y$. Assuming $y$ is between $u(a)$ and $u(b)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{Y}(y) &= P(Y \le y) \\
&= P(u(X) \le y) \\
&= P(X \le u^{-1}(y)) \\
&= \int_{a}^{u^{-1}(y)}f_{X}(t)dt \\
&= \left.F_{X}(t)\right|_{a}^{u^{-1}(y)} \\
&= F_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) - F_{X}(a)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we differentiate to get the probability density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= \frac{d}{dy}[F_{Y}(y)] \\
&= \frac{d}{dy}[F_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) - F_{X}(a)] \\
&= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y))(u^{-1})^{′}(y)
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $u$ is monotonically increasing, we have that $u^{-1}$ is monotonically increasing as well. To see this, it's helpful to remember that we reflect a function over the line $y=x$ to get its inverse.

Since the slope of a monotonically increasing function is always zero or positive, we have

$$
(u^{-1})'(y) \geq 0
$$

and consequently

$$
(u^{-1})'(y) = \left| (u^{-1})'(y) \right|
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{Y}(y) &= f_{X}(u^{-1}(y)) \mid (u^{-1})^{′}(y) \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "20e03906-77e2-525c-8b4e-ca6bd91782de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5449 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Change-of-Variables Formula"} :step/id #uuid "95cd8c7f-a4dd-5ba6-ad88-eab8ac6726e7" :step/math-academy-id 33927} {:db/id 17592186163272 :tutorial/content "Let's restate the change-of-variables method:

:question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
p_1(t)=t+1, \qquad
p_2(t)=t, \qquad
p_3(t)=t-1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}_1[t]$ of polynomials of degree $1$ or less in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t),q(t) \rangle =p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t+1,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t+1){|}_{-1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{-1}+(t+1){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1+1)\cdot (-1-1)+(1+1)\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{-1}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1-1)+(1)\cdot (1-1) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $p_2(t) \not\perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since $p_2(t) \not\perp p_3(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186134055 :question/id #uuid "97d43a34-aeb6-5e6a-8281-47dcdcd73020" :question/math-academy-id "q-100128" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id $$
{p}_{1}(t)=t-2,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t+2,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2t+4.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-2)q(-2)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,t+2⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot ((-2)+2)+(2-2)\cdot (2+2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2-2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t+2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t+2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t+2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =((-2)+2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2+2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =32\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(6)(-1)+2(0)(1)+3(-2)(-1) \\  & =-6+0+6 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(6)(1)+2(0)(1)+3(-2)(0) \\  & =6+0+0 \\  & =6\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${v}_{1}⊥̸{v}_{3},$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+4{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(4)(-8)+(-2)(4)+4(2)(5) \\  & =-32-8+40 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(1)+(-2)(2)+4(2)(0) \\  & =4-4+0 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(-8)(1)+(4)(2)+4(5)(0) \\  & =-8+8+0 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥̸{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =2(2)(1)+3(-1)(1)+(1)(-1) \\  & =4-3-1 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(1)(0)+3(1)(1)+(-1)(3) \\  & =0+3-3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(2)(0)+3(-1)(1)+(1)(3) \\  & =0-3+3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186133872 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133688 :question/id #uuid "dd873dd6-fdf6-50af-a080-abbb1800a096" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
f_1(t)=1, \qquad
f_2(t)=t, \qquad
f_3(t)=2t+1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
\langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨1,2t+1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}+t){|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & ={1}^{2}+1-((-1)^{2}+(-1)) \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,2t+1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2{t}^{2}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-(\frac{2(-1)^{3}}{3}+\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $f_2(t) \not\perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186134561 :question/id #uuid "2a5307a8-8a58-5d9f-8aa3-c19ff22a65ad" :question/math-academy-id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ))-\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =0+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186134569 :question/id #uuid "a07c5a93-5161-56bc-aa10-7d11733928e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99808" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15066878-30bb-508c-9db7-e8b10b72c732" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186133453} {:answer/id #uuid "1c2b7f86-e92f-5e2c-8860-4730a35f5501" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186133454} {:answer/id #uuid "29f32be0-6e29-59ac-a011-e3b3dd051fee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186133455} {:answer/id #uuid "73574aac-cbae-5bc4-ab25-5412b8255db1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186133456} {:answer/id #uuid "7a14430d-daac-5eb0-95da-dfa439a6fb71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186133457}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186133456} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e7eb080-b1fd-507d-8288-fb67ef87f7d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186133452}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$

$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{6}}{6}-\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{3},t⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-1)^{5}}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186272112 :question/id #uuid "0aa2e7ba-284c-52fb-a0ea-9a38be5541e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-140500" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={e}^{t},\,{f}_{3}(t)={e}^{-t}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-(e-{e}^{-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=-{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1}+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-({e}^{-1}-e) \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186272132 :question/id #uuid "1e4b04d4-e7d3-5042-809a-2a3512a7a902" :question/math-academy-id "q-140556"} {:db/id $$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{2}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,1⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡\alpha =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\alpha )}{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2}-(0-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -0-(0-0)] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}(t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-t){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-2-(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

:topic/math-academy-id 2104} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134813 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

![](images/69/69571997d87ed3f40ee7e9b0742075fbd5ee107892f6a9b4198f75f3f5a9fce3.svg)

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ &=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ &=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$

$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

![](images/69/69571997d87ed3f40ee7e9b0742075fbd5ee107892f6a9b4198f75f3f5a9fce3.svg)

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ &=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ &=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(2)+3(1)(2)+2(1)(-4)=2+6-8=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(-3)+3(1)(1)+2(1)(0)=-3+3+0=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(2)(-3)+3(2)(1)+2(-4)(0)=-6+6+0=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${V}$ is an orthogonal set." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f69210-8732-5a94-b16b-b7de520cfc66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "520866ac-288a-5e25-aa54-cc9335b03e13" :step/math-academy-id 32389 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134815}} {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$

"q-99827" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=1,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0$*

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t),$ ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ and ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "0052f793-89f1-5c58-93a6-48098b6aceba" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444801}} {:db/id 17592186444800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186380393 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "90f4b8b6-9087-5496-807d-608724aa78fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470631} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5fbf91-d7c1-5e8c-871e-7c26b0ac303e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470632}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470632} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b1dfa9f-9494-59d8-bf95-2c68f20b60a5" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471821} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f6085786-4948-5140-96cc-351034d2e7a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470633} {:answer/id #uuid "4fce3179-81d2-55bd-a37c-d2f3b28beee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470634}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470634} :answer-field/id #uuid "ffaaf373-8b01-5dda-82d5-b55d324b703d" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471822} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fecb31b-eea1-5984-a868-c589f3e59e53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470635} {:answer/id #uuid "0b89d20b-e663-5580-8552-4bead320d1f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470636}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470635} :answer-field/id #uuid "a51c31a2-df0f-5d9f-bff0-d622cce2a150" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb972e63-3e46-543b-9a40-0120a6183656" :question/math-academy-id "q-100120" :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t-4,\,{p}_{2}(t)=2-t,\,{p}_{3}(t)=1-t.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t-4,1-t⟩ \\  & =(2t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (1-t){|}_{1}+(2t-4){|}_{2}\cdot (1-t){|}_{2} \\  & =(2(1)-4)\cdot (1-1)+(2(2)-4)\cdot (1-2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2-t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(2-t){|}_{1}\cdot (1-t){|}_{1}+(2-t){|}_{2}\cdot (1-t){|}_{2} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (1-1)+(2-2)\cdot (1-2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t-4,2-t⟩ \\  & =(2t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (2-t){|}_{1}+(2t-4){|}_{2}\cdot (2-t){|}_{2} \\  & =(2(1)-4)\cdot (2-1)+(2(2)-4)\cdot (2-2) \\  & =-2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid "246bcb3d-ab36-5471-897e-d2a54e64c4f2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444803}} {:db/id 17592186444801 :step/content {:db/id 17592186237782 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4bc79c40-802c-5928-96bd-62b5abc8ad53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461159} {:answer/id #uuid "624f3dda-272a-59f4-81c4-afdc89b1b569" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461160} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1795204-45a0-5ae2-b1e0-fe24f1661e9a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462333} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d409008c-3927-5c03-9206-ddde6c3ce4c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461161} {:answer/id #uuid "1a4f7f7d-e705-5bea-b85e-15ecc20591e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461162}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461162} :answer-field/id #uuid "75ba454e-4199-5bbb-a3a5-a8496e22c83d" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462334} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10ce821b-8ac0-57db-b8d9-ccfbcbc7d8fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461163} {:answer/id #uuid "3128022b-3800-59d4-aea7-1dbf26659f5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461164}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461163} :answer-field/id #uuid "104242d5-dc4e-5e24-ac69-a557c354d5fa" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462335}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0e262e4d-a912-58d1-aa39-b29d3810a43d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100119" :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0e262e4d-a912-58d1-aa39-b29d3810a43d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100119" :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=t-2,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t+2,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2t+4.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-2)q(-2)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,t+2⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot ((-2)+2)+(2-2)\cdot (2+2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2-2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t+2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t+2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t+2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =((-2)+2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2+2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =32\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid "7719daea-6d1b-5000-8b05-8e73d08e6429" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444800}} {:db/id 17592186444800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186380393 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "90f4b8b6-9087-5496-807d-608724aa78fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470631} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5fbf91-d7c1-5e8c-871e-7c26b0ac303e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470632}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470632} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b1dfa9f-9494-59d8-bf95-2c68f20b60a5" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471821} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f6085786-4948-5140-96cc-351034d2e7a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470633} {:answer/id #uuid "4fce3179-81d2-55bd-a37c-d2f3b28beee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470634}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470634} :answer-field/id #uuid "ffaaf373-8b01-5dda-82d5-b55d324b703d" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471822} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fecb31b-eea1-5984-a868-c589f3e59e53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470635} {:answer/id #uuid "0b89d20b-e663-5580-8552-4bead320d1f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470636}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470635} :answer-field/id #uuid "a51c31a2-df0f-5d9f-bff0-d622cce2a150" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb972e63-3e46-543b-9a40-0120a6183656" :question/math-academy-id "q-100120" :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

"q-99656" :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(4)+2(1)(-1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =4-2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(0)+2(-1)(1)+2(1)(1) \\  & =0-2+2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(0)+2(1)(1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =0+2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "068d6b66-d519-5161-9eb3-7efaee833625" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518316}} {:db/id 17592186518233 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362397 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b37083a7-aaaa-5a2a-973a-5c9ff944dfe5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470032} {:answer/id #uuid "aade6615-cdec-5bb3-9ebc-b52ba6498acb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470033}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470033} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ee6465c-b492-5dcd-9a5b-72f46a3a5104" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470628} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8dcfb967-51e5-5257-b6ea-f6b21931da14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470034} {:answer/id #uuid "d6927137-4c46-5fd0-a3de-bc83e11cc13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470035}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470034} :answer-field/id #uuid "f55811ff-e66f-5a0e-812a-3b75349cc59e" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470629} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ec93396-6ade-5b54-b2dc-4c3f0308a1a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470036} {:answer/id #uuid "42e1db1a-4eb1-5170-b19b-b7d378bf5855" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470037}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470036} :answer-field/id #uuid "8547b10e-8dd7-5314-9138-e70dea301350" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d313e454-e9a2-5532-b1b1-37c4d7cbbe80" :question/math-academy-id "q-99951" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}(t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-t){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-2-(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(4)+2(1)(-1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =4-2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(0)+2(-1)(1)+2(1)(1) \\  & =0-2+2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(0)+2(1)(1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =0+2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "068d6b66-d519-5161-9eb3-7efaee833625" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518316}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(-1)q(-1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t+1,3t⟩ \\  & =(2t+1){|}_{0}\cdot (3t){|}_{0}+(2t+1){|}_{-1}\cdot (3t){|}_{-1} \\  & =(2(0)+1)\cdot (3(0))+(2(-1)+1)\cdot (3(-1)) \\  & =3\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨3t,t+1⟩ \\  & =(3t){|}_{0}\cdot (t+1){|}_{0}+(3t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =(3(0))\cdot (0+1)+(3(-1))\cdot ((-1)+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "b9cfa362-8135-55c9-a260-2d92a37de08c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518233}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\,v,\,v⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{8}u.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{8}u.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=v\,z=v} \\  & =({u}^{2}\cdot {u}^{2})\cdot {v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}\, \\  & ={u}^{4}{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}4xy\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=v,\,z=6-3u-2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 3.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,6-3u-2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =4xy\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=6-3u-2v} \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4xy\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot 4\cdot 9 \\  & =36\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186235462 :question/id #uuid "1a131946-3c50-5cb9-8c20-5138d22bf7c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-167649"} {:db/id 17592186278391 :question/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{S}(x+y+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,3v,\,2u-v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=3\sqrt{6}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=3\sqrt{6}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x+y+z)\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=3v\,z=2u-v} \\  & =(u+v)+(3v)+(2u-v) \\  & =3u+3v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(3u+3v)\cdot 3\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,(u+v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{0}^{1}u+v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =9\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+vu]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =9\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}+v)\text{d}v \\  & =9\sqrt{6}{[\frac{v}{2}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =9\sqrt{6}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186418478 :question/id #uuid "d41258e7-4727-5661-9adb-26ceb25d76d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-161185"} {:db/id 17592186540183 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 3386} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186173080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "44c6f181-59d4-55f2-b782-d9635d1f8d52"
