:tutorial/content "Consider a continuous scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ and a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined for $(u,v) \in D,$ where $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ 

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

 

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

 

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular.

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186173081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172130 44243} {:db/id 17592186173256 :tutorial/content "Consider a continuous scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ and a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined for $(u,v) \in D,$ where $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ 

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

 

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

 

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular. 

Let's see an example of applying this in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "31cee43f-e940-5add-90d5-831ffcaaafc8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7660 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186048327 *Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186486457 :question/id #uuid "f5101e52-f007-51fe-8d87-cde53f7bb6a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-146444" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "019c2c01-30dd-5c5f-8b90-73f9344dc881" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.25,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.0075" :db/id 17592186485766} {:answer/id #uuid "02fb1520-a9c6-5a73-a112-44948c9ae426" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.25,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.0085" :db/id 17592186485769} {:answer/id #uuid "1fc72d5e-57f2-5ca3-8e38-bf9dd994405d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.75,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.0075" :db/id 17592186485819} {:answer/id #uuid "37521a95-ddd5-5ea7-b2b3-b4bdd56c6670" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.25,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.0065" :db/id 17592186485870} {:answer/id #uuid "b6a5fb5b-749a-576d-91ab-0632592d5e04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.75,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.0065" :db/id 17592186486092}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485766} :answer-field/id #uuid "af58c111-f99a-57f4-a10e-1136008a2d5e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186486312}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Suppose that $25%$ of a high school student population like mathematics. *Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186486435 :question/id #uuid "bfc489e6-3fde-599d-8b94-fa54c6ab85f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-146400" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c6e9aa3-7579-5a88-aab9-009a45405b6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{Bernoulli}(0.42)" :db/id 17592186485844} {:answer/id #uuid "4d29a851-eb8b-501c-abce-b34ca4a45796" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B(66,0.42)" :db/id 17592186485907} {:answer/id #uuid "8bfb1579-730f-5017-931e-2e7002367e48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B(28,0.42)" :db/id 17592186486015} {:answer/id #uuid "b1bcdc0f-1389-5e8c-a2f7-0ffa32acc877" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B(66,0.58)" :db/id 17592186486083} {:answer/id #uuid "e0ae63a2-5d82-5b0e-b38b-f7334456bc5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{Bernoulli}(0.58)" :db/id 17592186486175}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485907} :answer-field/id #uuid "e4b6f92b-32ff-54a7-9dff-a149716ae98e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186486334}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=66$ from a population where $42%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. 17592186163117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$"

If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by

$$
p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6.
$$

In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$

Note the following:

- $N$ is the **population size**

- $p$ is the **population proportion**

- The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by

$$
Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30.
$$

In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas.

We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by

![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ 

Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward:

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\  & =\frac{Np}{N} \\  & =\frac{30}{50} \\  & =0.6\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example,

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ).
$$

To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\  & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\  & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\  & =\frac{29}{49} \\  & ≈0.592 \\  & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$

Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3fb9dab1-fabb-573d-8f7b-d06c37474163" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6461 :tutorial/title we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size.

The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. 

Let's now consider the following statistic:

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i
$$

where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ 

Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic.

We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following:

- Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$

- Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables.

- It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

We summarize this process using the following flow chart.

![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png)

Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77f66879-2dda-57f9-b96c-2ad1166282c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6477 :tutorial/title "The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic"} :step/id #uuid "7f0864d1-c890-56d0-ad56-9af735a0fb71" :step/math-academy-id 39212 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163120}} {:db/id 17592186163125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$

Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*.

This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. 

To see why, we first note that 

$$
P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5.
$$

Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\  & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\  & =\frac{499}{999} \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we've shown that

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1),
$$

suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "a129ef6b-606a-5b23-8f65-0573d4422fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6479 :tutorial/title "Independence in Large Populations"} :step/id #uuid "16f70a0f-60a9-55ce-a435-a9dd8530d4d9" :step/math-academy-id 39214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163124}} {:db/id 17592186163126 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows:

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i =  \overline{X}
$$

Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

 

Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\  & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\  & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important results:

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8ecb0abb-cc8a-58b3-b310-fabeeb9c4aca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6480 :tutorial/title "Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions"} :step/id #uuid "656c4a52-6bb0-59f8-878d-58db462b17ee" :step/math-academy-id 39215 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163128}} {:db/id 17592186163128 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$  is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}
$$

If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows:

$$
\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]  = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}
$$

Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :tutorial/id #uuid "34af16d9-40e0-5de6-9e2d-753be4cea679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6484 :tutorial/title "The Standard Error"} :step/id #uuid "8e2f6423-528f-586d-8112-c73e1f771a8a" :step/math-academy-id 39234 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163118}}] :activity/title "Sampling Proportions From Finite Populations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162231} {:db/id 17592186163117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$"

If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by

$$
p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6.
$$

In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$

Note the following:

- $N$ is the **population size**

- $p$ is the **population proportion**

- The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by

$$
Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30.
$$

In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas.

We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by

![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ 

Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward:

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\  & =\frac{Np}{N} \\  & =\frac{30}{50} \\  & =0.6\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example,

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ).
$$

To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\  & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\  & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\  & =\frac{29}{49} \\  & ≈0.592 \\  & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$

Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3fb9dab1-fabb-573d-8f7b-d06c37474163" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6461 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b7e31dee-05b0-5626-92d4-2ad066905c81" :step/math-academy-id 39024 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163119}} {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77f66879-2dda-57f9-b96c-2ad1166282c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6477 :tutorial/title "The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic"} :step/id #uuid "7f0864d1-c890-56d0-ad56-9af735a0fb71" :step/math-academy-id 39212 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163120}} {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size.

The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. 

Let's now consider the following statistic:

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i
$$

where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ 

Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic.

We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following:

- Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$

- Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables.

- It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

We summarize this process using the following flow chart.

![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png)

Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77f66879-2dda-57f9-b96c-2ad1166282c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6477 :tutorial/title "The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic"} {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$

Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*.

This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. 

To see why, we first note that 

$$
P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5.
$$

Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\  & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\  & =\frac{499}{999} \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we've shown that

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1),
$$

suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "a129ef6b-606a-5b23-8f65-0573d4422fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6479 :tutorial/title "Independence in Large Populations"} {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows:

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i =  \overline{X}
$$

Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

 

Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\  & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\  & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important results:

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8ecb0abb-cc8a-58b3-b310-fabeeb9c4aca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6480 :tutorial/title "Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions"} {:db/id 17592186163128 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$  is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}
$$

If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows:

$$
\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]  = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}
$$

Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :tutorial/id #uuid "34af16d9-40e0-5de6-9e2d-753be4cea679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6484 :tutorial/title "The Standard Error"} :step/id #uuid "8e2f6423-528f-586d-8112-c73e1f771a8a" :step/math-academy-id 39234 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163118}} {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$  is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$

{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "74a5ebf6-1c92-5485-bb12-c261b4d4f72a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486499}} {:db/id 17592186486499 :step/content {:db/id 17592186486446 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71ec1015-67ae-532c-90ae-ecdaface5f9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.4,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.012" :db/id 17592186485960} {:answer/id #uuid "a2dbf744-dd49-5c6d-a61b-984a7259504c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.6,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.018" :db/id 17592186486057} {:answer/id #uuid "adf531a6-7319-5b80-9274-0509621d73e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.6,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.024" :db/id 17592186486077} {:answer/id #uuid "cc4631fc-533d-5b33-96dd-c7fb0f7aac14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.4,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.024" :db/id 17592186486133} {:answer/id #uuid "fd23b3bb-07c4-5f49-97bc-5ab8e4e8d978" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.6,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=0.012" :db/id 17592186486227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186486227} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6c7b60b-ebc0-552f-bb22-591e7a44c23f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186486324}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d1024622-b9b9-5914-883d-61f4135d4db2" :question/math-academy-id "q-146442" :question/problem "Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. *Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$

$$

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)

A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "97e146b0-570c-5e63-97c5-a9b64f3bdfb7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486471}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71ec1015-67ae-532c-90ae-ecdaface5f9b" :answer/type {:db/id We say that $\mathbf{X}$ is a **bivariate normal vector** with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ if the joint probability density function of $\mathbf{X}$ is given by

$$
f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =[\begin{aligned}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

Here, 

- $\sigma^2_1 = \textrm{Var}[X_1]$ and $\sigma^2_2 = \textrm{Var}[X_2]$ are the variances of $X_1$ and $X_2,$

- $\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21} = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2]$ is the covariance of $X_1$ and $X_2$,

- $\rho$ is the linear correlation coefficient of $X_1$ and $X_2,$ and

- $|\Sigma|$ denotes the determinant of $\Sigma,$ the covariance matrix.

A graph of a typical density function of a bivariate normal vector is depicted below. 

![](images/d1/d195358d6dc5b7b8a1080d53c774ee4289ce0f97c17de3bf45a52e86c6b20e29.png)

17592186093238 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093482 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we compared the PDF of $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),$ given by 

$$
f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).
$$

and the joint PDF of a bivariate normal distribution $\mathbf X = [X_1,X_2]^T$ with mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ given by

$$
f(x_1, x_2) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}2}/2} {\color{blue}|\Sigma|}^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,{\color{blue}\Sigma}^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right).
$$

We can generalize this for an arbitrary number of variables ${\color{red}p},$ as follows:

$$
f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}p}/2} {\color{blue}|\Sigma|}^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,{\color{blue}\Sigma}^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)
$$

The function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p)$ is called the **multivariate normal** density function. A random vector $\mathbf X = [X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_p]^T$ with this joint density function is said to follow a **multivariate normal distribution**.

Similar to the bivariate case, we can consider linear combinations of coordinates of multivariate normal random vectors: 

*If $\mathbf{X} =  [X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k]^T$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as 

$$
Y= \mathbf c^T \mathbf X = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i X_i
$$

 is a normally distributed random variable, where $\mathbf c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and*

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ Var[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the expression for the variance is a quadratic form." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2ce75d0-2db0-5254-880f-d1042f119f29" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6998 :tutorial/title "The Multivariate Normal Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "f937d23e-c522-5623-bb89-f42667039185" :step/math-academy-id 42260 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093237}} {:db/id 17592186093239 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093483 :tutorial/content "Recall that a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2}.
$$

This probability density function can be written as 

$$
f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).
$$

Let's compare this to the density function of a bivariate normal vector. First, we rewrite the joint density $f(x_1,x_2)$ of the bivariate normal distribution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{|Σ|}}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu )) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-1}|Σ{|}^{-1/2}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu )) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-2/2}{|Σ|}^{-1/2}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu ))\end{aligned}
$$

By comparing the expressions for $f(x)$ and $f(x_1,x_2),$ we see that the *bivariate* normal distribution can be considered as a generalization of the *normal distribution* from the ${\color{red}1}$-dimensional case (when we have only one variable, $x$) to the ${\color{red}2}$-dimensional case (when we have two variables, $x_1$ and $x_2$).

This analogy will be particularly helpful when extending the bivariate normal distribution to more than two random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "198d2a80-9efc-509c-8852-d560b1203524" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7016 :tutorial/title "Normal Distribution vs. Bivariate Normal Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "56eb632e-0a3e-5c4c-a62a-0984c2a4a72a" :step/math-academy-id 42318 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093241}} {:db/id 17592186093240 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093484 :tutorial/content "A linear combination of coordinates of a bivariate normal random vector generates a (one-dimensional) normal distribution:

*If $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ given by*

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =[\begin{aligned}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

*then the random variable $Y,$ defined as *

$$
Y= aX_1 + bX_2
$$

*is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b.$ Furthermore, we have that*

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ Var[Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "62a410d8-f059-5273-ba3a-15646c153a7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7017 :tutorial/title "Linear Combinations of Normal Random Variables From Bivariate Distributions"} :step/id #uuid "35262d1e-3ec3-5c70-a2dc-cca3fc1c3e76" :step/math-academy-id 42319 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093236}} {:db/id 17592186093241 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093485 :tutorial/content "Let's consider a bivariate normal vector $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right),
$$

where the mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =[\begin{aligned}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Most of the parameters of the distribution can be interpreted geometrically on a corresponding graph of the probability density function:

- The mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ gives the $xy$-coordinates of the peak.

- The correlation coefficient $\rho$ defines how much the bell is squeezed towards the plane $y=x{:}$ 

- when $\rho \to 0,$ the horizontal cross-sections are almost circular, while

- when $\rho \to 1,$ the shape becomes more and more squeezed towards the plane $y=x.$

![](images/5b/5bd69db417134cccedd5af45cb56fb44f27925ba5a8470f3b5622f0856ed855d.png)

 

- The variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ represent how much the curve is spread out along the principal axes $x_1=\mu_1$ and $x_2=\mu_2{:}$

- when $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are small, the bell shape is more "pointy," while

- for larger $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2,$ the bell shape is more "flat."

The level curves of the surface have equations of the form

$$
(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu) = \textrm{const},
$$

 

which represent ellipses centered at $(\mu_1,\mu_2).$

and the joint PDF of a bivariate normal distribution $\mathbf X = [X_1,X_2]^T$ with mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ given by

$$

$$

The function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p)$ is called the **multivariate normal** density function. A random vector $\mathbf X = [X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_p]^T$ with this joint density function is said to follow a **multivariate normal distribution**.

 is a normally distributed random variable, where $\mathbf c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and*

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ Var[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}

Notice that the expression for the variance is a quadratic form." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2ce75d0-2db0-5254-880f-d1042f119f29" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6998 :tutorial/title "The Multivariate Normal Distribution"} {:db/id 17592186093483 :tutorial/content "Recall that a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2}.
$$

This probability density function can be written as 

$$
f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).
$$

Let's compare this to the density function of a bivariate normal vector. First, we rewrite the joint density $f(x_1,x_2)$ of the bivariate normal distribution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{|Σ|}}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu )) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-1}|Σ{|}^{-1/2}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu )) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-2/2}{|Σ|}^{-1/2}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu ))\end{aligned}
$$

By comparing the expressions for $f(x)$ and $f(x_1,x_2),$ we see that the *bivariate* normal distribution can be considered as a generalization of the *normal distribution* from the ${\color{red}1}$-dimensional case (when we have only one variable, $x$) to the ${\color{red}2}$-dimensional case (when we have two variables, $x_1$ and $x_2$).

This analogy will be particularly helpful when extending the bivariate normal distribution to more than two random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "198d2a80-9efc-509c-8852-d560b1203524" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7016 :tutorial/title "Normal Distribution vs. Bivariate Normal Distribution"} {:db/id 17592186093241 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093485 :tutorial/content "Let's consider a bivariate normal vector $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right),
$$

where the mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =[\begin{aligned}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Most of the parameters of the distribution can be interpreted geometrically on a corresponding graph of the probability density function:

- The mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ gives the $xy$-coordinates of the peak.

- The correlation coefficient $\rho$ defines how much the bell is squeezed towards the plane $y=x{:}$ 

- when $\rho \to 0,$ the horizontal cross-sections are almost circular, while

- when $\rho \to 1,$ the shape becomes more and more squeezed towards the plane $y=x.$

![](images/5b/5bd69db417134cccedd5af45cb56fb44f27925ba5a8470f3b5622f0856ed855d.png)

 

- The variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ represent how much the curve is spread out along the principal axes $x_1=\mu_1$ and $x_2=\mu_2{:}$

- when $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are small, the bell shape is more "pointy," while

- for larger $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2,$ the bell shape is more "flat."

The level curves of the surface have equations of the form

$$
(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu) = \textrm{const},
$$

 

which represent ellipses centered at $(\mu_1,\mu_2).$

$$

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $a$ and $b$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}+(8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186491172 :question/id #uuid "82932d5f-4a58-5db1-a173-dc03ee3fc19c" :question/math-academy-id "q-133835"} {:db/id 17592186498515 :question/id #uuid According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & ={c}^{2}-{b}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $b$ and $c$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\sqrt{(13)^{2}-(12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{169-144} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186489267 :question/id #uuid "ce23a05a-85d4-5790-9eda-0cc10c821050" :question/math-academy-id "q-5650" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a9cdac2-f621-564f-8709-0203bdf85dd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{35}{2}" :db/id 17592186488589} {:answer/id #uuid "60d53825-bf07-5091-90ed-8b078be85249" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{873}{2}}" :db/id 17592186488656} {:answer/id #uuid "79751c18-eaa3-5051-9226-7e74700d3de0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186488710} {:answer/id #uuid "7c96d7b0-33e5-5715-9230-bacb2c9fa936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186488719} {:answer/id #uuid "ac564bf3-c6f3-5221-811b-35794c5d512f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{323}" :db/id 17592186488810}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186488710} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a817628-1149-5ae9-912f-5d3dd1012acd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186489091}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/3c/3c5b5a5c9531b6568c78633f5c44c8332cc722c9d88860a4b6bb9c2c336a1683.png)

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $VY=WY$ and $VZ=WZ.$" :question/worked-solution "By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Here, the points $Y$ and $Z$ are both equidistant from the endpoints of $\overset{―}{VW}.$ Therefore, $Y$ and $Z$ both  lie on the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{VW}.$    

Since only one line can be drawn through two given points, the line $\overset{⟷}{YZ}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{VW}.$ 

In particular, we have that $VX=WX.$ We can use this equation to solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}VX & =WX \\ 4x-2 & =2x+4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549029 :question/id #uuid "8e4299a8-dbfe-5e92-9aa9-392339c4eb42" :question/math-academy-id "q-76794" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a509626-e980-52d1-8ac6-b779e420ad7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186548376} {:answer/id #uuid "1fe152df-c056-56e4-8835-05f63b7ca375" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186548415} {:answer/id #uuid "5595a2b1-93ac-5938-9351-2e8f17025a42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186548515} {:answer/id #uuid "7db77d85-a0dc-5dc2-a4db-a208a7e4e24b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186548592} {:answer/id #uuid "824ef6d0-40cc-5ffb-90ae-9f5f0cac548b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186548604}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548592} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc772387-bb72-5d5b-abe3-ac9a76d448eb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548948}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/f0/f07faaa85e166b53068db13609fd10958dfe4857df5118188be3ca709e6e0b8b.png)

$$

$$
(a+b)^{n}.

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16})(1)+4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8})(4)+6(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(16) \\  & \,+4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
(a+b)^{n}.

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=1,$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(1)^{4}(-{z}^{2})^{0}+4(1)^{3}(-{z}^{2})^{1}+6(1)^{2}(-{z}^{2})^{2}+4(1)^{1}(-{z}^{2})^{3}+1(1)^{0}(-{z}^{2})^{4} \\  & =1(1)(1)+4(1)(-{z}^{2})+6(1)({z}^{4})+4(1)(-{z}^{6})+1(1)({z}^{8}) \\  & =1-4{z}^{2}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{6}+{z}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
(1-{z}^{2})^{4}={z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{2}+1
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

$$
{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}.

"Given that 

$$
{(2{t}^{2}-3s)}^{4}=A{t}^{8}+B{t}^{6}s+C{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2{t}^{2},$ and $b=-3s.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{t}^{2}-3s)^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(2{t}^{2})}^{4}(-3s)^{0}+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{3}(-3s)^{1}+6{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}(-3s)^{2} \\  & \,+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{1}(-3s)^{3}+1{(2{t}^{2})}^{0}(-3s)^{4} \\  & =1(16{t}^{8})(1)+4(8{t}^{6})(-3s)+6(4{t}^{4})(9{s}^{2}) \\  & \,+4(2{t}^{2})(-27{s}^{3})+1(1)(81{s}^{4}) \\  & =16{t}^{8}-96{t}^{6}s+216{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=16,B=-96,$ and $C=216.$ Finally,

$$
A+B+C=16-96+216=136.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503741 :question/id #uuid "c989ddc2-999c-5079-ab1b-dc05c9512624" :question/math-academy-id "q-12884" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bac5b62-4ee8-545a-966d-5c12ee806664" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x-10y{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503009} {:answer/id #uuid "24ced81d-498a-516a-95d5-fb01dede7a9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x+3y{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503051} {:answer/id #uuid "5e2cc4e3-3a7b-5190-9ba6-ed8c80cfcd59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x-6y{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503165} {:answer/id #uuid "6331dd90-d13b-5bdb-bc74-b83aa99db890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{3}-4{y}^{2}x+10y{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503172} {:answer/id #uuid "c137176e-2ac9-58c5-84bd-949dafa76422" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{3}-4{y}^{2}x+6y{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503368}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503051} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b892af4-e657-5e7b-967c-44dc67970e0b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503583}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find, in descending powers of $y$ and ascending powers of $x,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(y-x)}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=3,$ $a=y,$ and $b=-x.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{3}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{3}.
$$

The $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,3,3,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(y-x)}^{3} & =1{a}^{3}+3{a}^{2}b+3a{b}^{2}+1{b}^{3} \\  & =1(y)^{3}(-x)^{0}+3(y)^{2}(-x)^{1}+3(y)^{1}(-x)^{2}+1(y)^{0}(-x)^{3} \\  & =1({y}^{3})(1)+3({y}^{2})(-x)+3(y)({x}^{2})+1(1)(-{x}^{3}) \\  & ={y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x+3y{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $y$ and ascending powers of $x,$ the first three terms are

$$
{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x+3y{x}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548014 :question/id #uuid "700411f4-106e-5592-a547-8738d64ef693" :question/math-academy-id "q-110676" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "209aed4f-131b-523e-a4e8-1446b6171323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186547382} {:answer/id #uuid "3bcbebd1-5d2a-5581-b48c-489d2c32892b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186547446} {:answer/id #uuid "43b9c880-5fa3-575f-adb6-b7776ccb3b8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24" :db/id 17592186547467} {:answer/id #uuid "47d804d7-6d7b-51dc-82a8-e898d3670e24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186547476} {:answer/id #uuid "ad8e8633-e525-5531-b1dd-16c1c9c6e25e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186547696}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547476} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe5bbd0a-c356-5392-bd90-c3fba4a83d1d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547966}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that

$$
(a+b)^{n}.

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2s-{u}^{2})^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{4} \\  & =1(2s)^{4}{(-{u}^{2})}^{0}+4(2s)^{3}{(-{u}^{2})}^{1}+6(2s)^{2}{(-{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & \,+4(2s)^{1}{(-{u}^{2})}^{3}+1(2s)^{0}{(-{u}^{2})}^{4} \\  & =1(16{s}^{4})(1)+4(8{s}^{3})(-{u}^{2})+6(4{s}^{2})({u}^{4}) \\  & \,+4(2s)(-{u}^{6})+1(1)({u}^{8}) \\  & =16{s}^{4}-32{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+24{s}^{2}{u}^{4}-8s{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}}=$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the radical $\sqrt{5}$ from the denominator, all we need to do is multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{5}$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{5}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{5}}{5} & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the product rule to simplify the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{5}}{5} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3\cdot 5}}{5} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{15}}{5} & \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495125 :question/id #uuid "ae109d24-9fc2-5d5a-8052-a06c5bb12363" :question/math-academy-id "q-68978" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6f7a6999-f8f4-59e0-98e0-015a493f1d2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{21}}{7}" :db/id 17592186494555} {:answer/id #uuid "89a01196-ecc5-54e7-97a0-a62b76df60ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\sqrt{7}}{7}" :db/id 17592186494626} {:answer/id #uuid "9af2d328-e266-562e-9983-62f0ac8950e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{63}}{7}" :db/id 17592186494673} {:answer/id #uuid "c52da2ef-45c8-5cc1-8d40-dcc039628f7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}" :db/id 17592186494781} {:answer/id #uuid "e2e5fe20-ac58-5d90-b58b-91cc21887122" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{7}}{21}" :db/id 17592186494859}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494555} :answer-field/id #uuid "a3bf9e83-273c-5b34-b405-581696dd025a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494994}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{7}}=$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the radical $\sqrt{7}$ from the denominator, all we need to do is multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{7}$ and simplify:

"Consider the equation

$$
(p-3)x=4x
$$

where $p$ is a constant. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $p?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax=bx
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a=b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax=bx.$ In this case, 

$$
a=p-3,\,b=4.
$$

Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
p-3=4.
$$

Solving this for $p,$ we get

$$
p=7.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186297170 :question/id #uuid "e508284d-0585-5c0f-a542-d91d66f78ddf" :question/math-academy-id "q-287975"} {:db/id 17592186297183 :question/id #uuid {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax+b=cx+d
$$

where $a,b,c,$ and $d$ are constants. This equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a=c\,\text{and}\,b=d.
$$

To determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation

$$
(-s+3)x+2t=x+6
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we equate the coefficients of $x,$ and we equate the constants:

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
-s+3=1.
$$

Solving this equation for $s,$ we get

$$
s=2.
$$

- Equating the constants, we have

$$
2t=6.
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
t=3.
$$

Finally, since $s=2$ and $t=3,$ we have

$$
s+t=2+3=5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186297198 :question/id #uuid "afc322c5-285c-5560-a114-d1da26bf18af" :question/math-academy-id "q-288622"} {:db/id 17592186297199 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following equations has *no* solution?

I. $|5z+1|=5$

II. $|5z+1|-3=-1$

III. $|5z+1|=-6$" :question/worked-solution "An absolute value equation has no solution if, when the absolute value is isolated on the left side, the right-hand side is negative.

With that in mind, let's look at each equation in turn:

- Equation I has a solution. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is non-negative.

- Equation II has a solution. To see this, we first isolate the absolute value on the left-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5z+1|-3 & =-1 \\ |5z+1| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-hand side is non-negative, this equation has a solution.

- Equation III *has no solution*. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is *negative*.

Therefore, the answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186192636 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192594 :question/id #uuid "de2efe4f-e236-5fb2-bc46-eb037ecf26b1" $$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $x=\frac{7}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186550006 :question/id #uuid "e2cc5506-dc0b-5a5b-8907-9924a3a993c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-215510"} {:db/id 17592186048517} {:db/id 17592186049005} {:db/id 17592186049258} {:db/id 17592186049309} {:activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186111733} :activity/id #uuid "9857734b-5bab-54f4-a580-a7385aea30f3" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048174 :topic/id #uuid "85adbb4a-1472-583d-a6f0-528ebb0b39cc" :topic/math-academy-id 1437} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186111609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110670 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110291 :question/id #uuid "60df6f7a-5257-5081-ba0c-0e9499a15f23" :question/math-academy-id "e-10588"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ac4127f-1253-5aee-b524-84e5c6b2bc64" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048673} {:db/id 17592186050452} {:db/id 17592186050494}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111241} {:db/id 17592186111279} {:db/id 17592186233215} {:db/id 17592186493947} {:db/id 17592186493950}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Angles From Right, Straight, and Full Angles Using Algebra"} :step/id #uuid "9d2f5fba-20ef-5cac-9659-5aee4c02e5a5" :step/math-academy-id 40025 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111742}} {:db/id 17592186111733 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111840 :tutorial/content "When solving problems with angles, it is helpful to remember the following classifications:

- a **null** angle has a measure of $0^\circ,$

- an **acute** angle has a measure between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ,$

- a **right** angle has a measure of $90^\circ,$

- an **obtuse** angle has a measure between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ,$

- a **straight** angle has a measure of $180^\circ,$

- a **reflex** angle has a measure between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ,$ and

- a **full** angle has a measure of $360^\circ.$

It is also helpful to remember that when two lines meet at a point, the opposite angles are called **vertical angles**. Vertical angles are congruent, and consequently they have the same measure." :tutorial/id #uuid "282e8601-d3f4-5c34-a96b-a071a96de244" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2182 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} Pascal's triangle is made by rows of numbers that form a triangle.
Each row has one more number than the row above.
The first two rows are made of three $1$s in a triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Let's construct the next row.
The first and last number in each row is always $1.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & ◻ &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The other numbers are always greater than $1$ and can be found by adding the two closest numbers located in the previous row.

In our case, the numbers closest to the unknown number and located in the previous row are ${\color{blue}1}$ and ${\color{blue}1}.$
Therefore, the unknown number is the sum of $\color{blue}1$ and ${\color{blue}1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
{\large\square} = {\color{blue}1} + {\color{blue}1} = 2
$$

Now, we have the first three rows of Pascal's triangle.

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

If we continue repeating this process for each row, we will get the following results for the first six rows of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}

Let's consider the binomial expansion of 

$$

where $n$ is a positive integer.

To write out the expansion, we use two patterns to simplify most of the hard work: the **exponent pattern** and the **coefficient pattern**.

- The **exponent pattern** is
 

$$
a^{\color{red}n}b^{\color{blue}0},\quad  a^{\color{red}{n-1}}b^{{\color{blue}1}}, \quad   a^{{\color{red}n-2}}b^{\color{blue}2}, \quad  \dots\quad   a^{\color{red}2}b^{{\color{blue}n-2}},\quad    a^{\color{red}1}b^{{\color{blue}n - 1}}, \quad   a^{\color{red}0}b^{{\color{blue}n}}.
$$

The exponents of $a$ start at $n$ and go down ($n, n-1, \cdots, 1, 0$) while the exponents of $b$ increase from $0$ to $n.$ In every term, the two exponents always add up to $n.$

- The **coefficient pattern** can be found using Pascal's Triangle:
 

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

We take the top row to be the $0$th row. Then, the $n$th row of Pascal's Triangle are the coefficients of $(a+b)^n.$

Let's use this to expand the binomial 

$$
(a+b)^3.
$$

The exponent pattern is

$$
a^{\color{red}3}b^{\color{blue}0},\quad  a^{\color{red}2}b^{\color{blue}1}, \quad a^{\color{red}1}b^{\color{blue}2}, \quad  a^{\color{red}0}b^{\color{blue}3}.
$$

Since $n=3,$ the coefficient pattern is found using the $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle: $(1,3,3,1).$

$$
(a + b)^3  
= \mathbf{1}a^{\color{red}3}b^{\color{blue}0} + \mathbf{3}a^{\color{red}2}b^{\color{blue}1} + \mathbf{3}a^{\color{red}1}b^{\color{blue}2} + \mathbf{1}a^{\color{red}0}b^{\color{blue}3}.

$$

:activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186101026} {:db/id 17592186101573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101977 :tutorial/content "One interesting number pattern is **Pascal's triangle**, named after Blaise Pascal, a famous French mathematician.

Pascal's triangle is made by rows of numbers that form a triangle.
Each row has one more number than the row above.
The first two rows are made of three $1$s in a triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Let's construct the next row.
The first and last number in each row is always $1.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & ◻ &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The other numbers are always greater than $1$ and can be found by adding the two closest numbers located in the previous row.

In our case, the numbers closest to the unknown number and located in the previous row are ${\color{blue}1}$ and ${\color{blue}1}.$
Therefore, the unknown number is the sum of $\color{blue}1$ and ${\color{blue}1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
{\large\square} = {\color{blue}1} + {\color{blue}1} = 2
$$

Now, we have the first three rows of Pascal's triangle.

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

If we continue repeating this process for each row, we will get the following results for the first six rows of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f708f697-814a-58cd-8926-d278c8e15fc4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3392 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9bab1b86-237d-59f2-b5b8-117d4edfdf46" :step/math-academy-id 105243 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101574}} {:db/id 17592186101977 :tutorial/content "One interesting number pattern is **Pascal's triangle**, named after Blaise Pascal, a famous French mathematician.

:db/id 17592186503516}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ab532852-8985-56d4-9487-9412ea181516" :question/math-academy-id "q-3564" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{(2{t}^{2}-3s)}^{4}=A{t}^{8}+B{t}^{6}s+C{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2{t}^{2},$ and $b=-3s.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{t}^{2}-3s)^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(2{t}^{2})}^{4}(-3s)^{0}+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{3}(-3s)^{1}+6{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}(-3s)^{2} \\  & \,+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{1}(-3s)^{3}+1{(2{t}^{2})}^{0}(-3s)^{4} \\  & =1(16{t}^{8})(1)+4(8{t}^{6})(-3s)+6(4{t}^{4})(9{s}^{2}) \\  & \,+4(2{t}^{2})(-27{s}^{3})+1(1)(81{s}^{4}) \\  & =16{t}^{8}-96{t}^{6}s+216{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=16,B=-96,$ and $C=216.$ Finally,

$$
A+B+C=16-96+216=136.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0fcd4859-f70e-5b53-af4b-3bf056bd41ce" :step/next {:db/id 17592186503841}} {:db/id 17592186503805 :step/content {:db/id 17592186503745 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b600bcd-5006-5baf-9dca-4aab5033031d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+125{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503008} {:answer/id #uuid "4c839c43-5c26-510d-85ac-e2e3c39a216c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503128} {:answer/id #uuid "4fb998d5-d716-53e2-a50b-72e1271eb277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}-100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503133} {:answer/id #uuid "5135b701-cd58-5dde-8d9b-989995318cb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503136} {:answer/id #uuid "9799692b-0119-5014-ae4f-3ef5e9145c63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503281}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503008} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef1b5443-9d42-51aa-ac69-73ecc6958d74" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503635}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d6a9fa51-d96f-5308-9675-af7e9df7f105" :question/math-academy-id "q-3563" :question/problem "Find, in ascending powers of $y,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(10y+\frac{1}{2})}^{5}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

:question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=3,$ $a=y,$ and $b=-x.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{3}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{3}.
$$

The $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,3,3,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(y-x)}^{3} & =1{a}^{3}+3{a}^{2}b+3a{b}^{2}+1{b}^{3} \\  & =1(y)^{3}(-x)^{0}+3(y)^{2}(-x)^{1}+3(y)^{1}(-x)^{2}+1(y)^{0}(-x)^{3} \\  & =1({y}^{3})(1)+3({y}^{2})(-x)+3(y)({x}^{2})+1(1)(-{x}^{3}) \\  & ={y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x+3y{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $y$ and ascending powers of $x,$ the first three terms are

$$
{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}x+3y{x}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "febb20a8-7bec-598d-9521-3df7ff50a618"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b600bcd-5006-5baf-9dca-4aab5033031d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, find the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ and $b=4.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16})(1)+4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8})(4)+6(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(16) \\  & \,+4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $A=\frac{1}{16},B=2$ and $C=24.$ So, finally

$$
A+B+C=\frac{1}{16}+2+24=\frac{417}{16}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a849bf07-e1b9-58de-b318-85fa4f3d86aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186548176}} {:db/id 17592186548176 :step/content {:db/id 17592186548051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7869ea61-e97c-524e-a14d-1788d8383e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547577} {:answer/id #uuid "863fbced-ba48-51fa-ac1c-071cd8741980" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}+2{z}^{6}-6{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547605} {:answer/id #uuid "a2e736b8-e40c-51d3-9a0e-4ad64eae66bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+18{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547671} {:answer/id #uuid "bbf1cdb0-233a-556a-92fd-fadf68dcfca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+12{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547718} {:answer/id #uuid "fd90e06c-4204-5316-a4d6-0173539fd070" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}+2{z}^{6}-4{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547838}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547577} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9807bbb-6450-5bec-9d6e-2cb5e0bc2c61" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547924}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c9b934c2-8c57-56f1-8a65-42f138da7b11" :question/math-academy-id "q-12891" :question/problem "Find, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(1-{z}^{2})}^{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=1,$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(1)^{4}(-{z}^{2})^{0}+4(1)^{3}(-{z}^{2})^{1}+6(1)^{2}(-{z}^{2})^{2}+4(1)^{1}(-{z}^{2})^{3}+1(1)^{0}(-{z}^{2})^{4} \\  & =1(1)(1)+4(1)(-{z}^{2})+6(1)({z}^{4})+4(1)(-{z}^{6})+1(1)({z}^{8}) \\  & =1-4{z}^{2}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{6}+{z}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
(1-{z}^{2})^{4}={z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{2}+1
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

$$
{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de2d3f8a-b796-5c4a-80a9-88cbe5bf41a1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186548180}} {:db/id 17592186548180 :step/content {:db/id 17592186548014 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "209aed4f-131b-523e-a4e8-1446b6171323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186547382} {:answer/id #uuid "3bcbebd1-5d2a-5581-b48c-489d2c32892b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186547446} {:answer/id #uuid "43b9c880-5fa3-575f-adb6-b7776ccb3b8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24" :db/id 17592186547467} {:answer/id #uuid "47d804d7-6d7b-51dc-82a8-e898d3670e24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186547476} {:answer/id #uuid "ad8e8633-e525-5531-b1dd-16c1c9c6e25e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186547696}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547476} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe5bbd0a-c356-5392-bd90-c3fba4a83d1d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547966}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "700411f4-106e-5592-a547-8738d64ef693" :question/math-academy-id "q-110676" :question/problem "Given that

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
